## PT-1671 -- STUDY 32: BG3 IS THE COUNTER-EXAMPLE TO STUDY 31, NOT A CONFIRMATION. BG3 HAS AN EXPLICIT COMBAT SESSION

BG3 has a real combat object: CombatantsOverlay binds to SelectedCharacter.Combat.Participants, CurrentCombat is nullable and gates the overlay's existence, and a StatusPropertyFlags valuelist names InitiateCombat, BringIntoCombat, AllowLeaveCombat, AllowLeaveDisallowJoinCombat. "BringIntoCombat" is decisive -- you cannot bring something into a non-container.

AND THE PANEL BINDS TO THE ROSTER, NOT VISIBILITY -- scoped negative across three files for every visibility term, none found. You can fight what you cannot see and it stays listed. Opposite of KOTOR.

Leaving is explicit and gated: "Flee from Combat" with three named failure reasons, including a DISTANCE gate and an EXTRACTION DESTINATION requirement. KOTOR's exit is free, ungated, usually fired by a conversation ending combat outright. That gap is the cost of BG3's roster.

RESEARCHER CORRECTED ITS OWN STUDY 31 SECTION 6: "no roster, do not build one" was argued from a real-time anchor. Turn order is why BG3 needs one -- "whose turn is next" is a question about an ORDERED SEQUENCE, and that conclusion does not survive contact with a turn-based game, which is what we are.

BUT the query-versus-store distinction survives intact: a roster and a STORED MUTABLE roster are different things. Joining and leaving are events; the list is a fold. PLAY-STATE-01 already works this way for everything else, and CombatParticipantsChangedCommand shows BG3's own UI treating membership as event-driven too, not as a flat list it owns.

AND: do not make visibility the membership rule. KOTOR's disengage-on-lost-sight is a real-time answer; on a grid it would let a player break combat by stepping behind a pillar. Show who is in the fight; treat visible as a DISPLAY PROPERTY of a row, not a filter on the list -- otherwise "gone" and "hidden" render identically, which is absence-versus-blank in a new place.

Transferable UX rather than mechanic: BG3 names WHY you cannot leave. Steal that habit, not the specific flee rules -- same shape as STUDY 21's Cause field.

NOT CHECKED, NAMED: the actual combat-start trigger is engine code in both games and was not found in either study. Whether BG3's Combatants list is filtered upstream of the UI layer. No Osiris script read.

## PT-1672 -- COMBAT ROSTER IS A FOLD OVER EVENTS, AND VISIBILITY IS A ROW PROPERTY, NOT A FILTER. Owner ruling, on STUDY 31/32

We are turn-based, so KOTOR's no-roster answer does not apply -- ordering a turn sequence is inherently roster-shaped, per Researcher's own correction at STUDY 32. But the roster is not a stored mutable list either: joining and leaving combat are events, and "who is in this fight right now" is a QUERY against the log, the same way PLAY-STATE-01 derives every other fact. encounter.began/encounter.ended already exist as event kinds; membership is a fold over them, not a new field anyone mutates directly.

RULED: every combatant that has joined the fight and not yet left it appears as a row on the panel for the fight's duration. A combatant that goes out of sight is NOT removed from the panel -- the row stays and is marked hidden.

Reason: an absence has to mean one thing. If "not shown" could mean dead, fled, out of sight, or never present, neither a player nor a test can tell which happened. PT-1551 already solved this exact problem for placements on the board -- a hidden creature holds its square and is marked, rather than omitted -- and this is the same rule one level up, applied to the roster instead of the board. Showing the row costs nothing extra; dropping it costs the distinction entirely.

And it is the safer failure mode specifically because we are turn-based: if a hidden enemy still has a turn coming, a player needs to see that a turn is coming for something, even while they cannot currently target it. Dropping the row would let a turn arrive with no warning anything was there.

Corrects the owner's earlier phrasing ("every visible enemy") to "every combatant in the fight, visibility as a per-row property" -- functionally close to what was asked, but a hidden combatant's row persists rather than disappearing.

## PT-1673 -- LOOTING BUILT. AND THE MARKER RULE HAD ALREADY STOPPED BEING TRUE -- A REGRESSION, CAUGHT BY ASKING THE CODE INSTEAD OF THE RULING

PT-1525/1521 said a dead creature is removed from the board. Half of that held: _stillHere correctly removes it from _here at both moments a creature can die -- not bumped into, not in the fight, not in the panel, its square vacated. But the token was still being PAINTED on the square it died on, under the player's own marker.

The cause: Lens paints area.contents, the file's placements, skipping only what concealed names -- and concealed was built by iterating _here. A creature removed from _here can no longer be NAMED there, so the renderer never learned it was gone. The filter and the renderer could not both be right, and the wrong one was the one nobody had asked, because the rule was applied to the list that decides who ACTS, not the list the board draws from.

AND THE EXISTING TEST COULD NOT SEE IT: nothing_dies_test's case built its own list IN THE TEST FILE, re-implementing _stillHere's predicate, and asserted the dead creature was not in ITS OWN COPY. It proved stateOf answers dead. Nothing had ever asked the board. Green throughout -- a rigorous check aimed at the wrong subject. Kept, now labelled with what it does and does not cover.

Fixed: the fallen come from the log, the one place that still knows. combatantFrom now carries the placement tag, so a death names WHICH creature died, not which kind.

RULED: closed as a regression, not new scope. Move to remains.

## PT-1674 -- LOOTING: REMAINS ARE A PROJECTION, THE VERB WAS ALREADY THERE, AND EVERY OPEN QUESTION WAS ANSWERED BY A DOCUMENT

Remains are runtime state, not a package write -- AREA-FORMAT-01 4 bars the engine from editing a package, so nothing is written into [[contents]]; a pile exists because the log says a creature died there and has not said its things were taken. Tag is the PLACEMENT that died, not the blueprint's handle. Position: character.died now carries x and y, since ENGINE-SPEC-04 4 writes no position during a round and a creature a doctrine walked could die somewhere its file never mentions -- a death written before it did falls back to the authored square, stated rather than silently exact.

ONCE LOOTED IT DISAPPEARS -- asked to pick and say why, and did: an empty pile IS an empty pile whichever way it got that way. Drawing one after looting but not before would contradict the owner's own no-pile-for-nothing rule, and a marker whose only meaning is "you already looted this" is a memory aid, not a fixture. And it needs no second state anywhere -- "stays, empty" requires a stored flag, which 4 will not let persist into a package and a projection gets for free. Cost named plainly: a looted square and a square where nothing died look the same.

THE VERB WAS ALREADY THERE. Step already means three things by where you step -- into a creature talks or fights, onto a door travels. A pile is the fourth; a pick-up key would be a second affordance on a board with one. And ACTION-ECONOMY-01 5 already names picking up among six free interactions, so "loot mid-fight or only after" was already answered by a document -- picking up is a free interaction, done on your turn, nothing invented. AND it makes 5's second sentence reachable for the first time: _interactionToll's own comment records that no second interaction was reachable in a fight, because speak cannot be taken and a door abandons the fight holding the counter. Two piles inside one turn's movement is a second interaction that does not end the round -- machinery kept for that day now has a caller.

THE LOG: item.acquired, one per item, campaign lifetime, declared since the vocabulary was written and emitted by nothing until now. Carries subject (looter), item (blueprint path, PT-1452), from (the pile's placement tag), area. A transfer is ONE event -- an item.lost for the corpse beside it would be two writers for one crossing, PT-1421, the defect PT-1626 paid for. What is left in the pile is DERIVED, not written. item.lost deliberately gets no constant and no fold -- nothing takes an item away yet, and a fold for a kind nobody writes is PT-1523's character.moved shape, which check_event_producers was built to catch.

PT-1266 minded: single log, single writer. _take hands events up rather than touching a file, and goes through _persist rather than writing onAppend directly -- _persist's own comment names every earlier site that hand-picked its own kinds instead.

TAKE-ALL, and the two open questions collapse into one: a chooser needs to show what you left behind, which is the empty pile already ruled out. Take-all needs no second state; named as a choice rather than a limitation -- the day inventory has weight or a limit, a chooser is what that change is for. And re-interacting with looted remains falls out for free: nothing to re-interact with, the square is ordinary.

RULED: closed. Every open question from the original brief was answered by an existing document rather than invented -- ACTION-ECONOMY-01, AREA-FORMAT-01, PT-1452, PT-1421, PT-1266, SAVE-LOAD-01, all already on record before this slice started.

## PT-1675 -- INTERRUPT IS BUILT CORRECTLY AND CURRENTLY DEAD CODE FROM THE PLAYER'S SIDE. PT-1534's GAP NOW BLOCKS A SHIPPED FEATURE

Tester confirmed the interrupt mechanism against the reader before touching the app: the legality gate (interrupt only on a then-continuing line) refuses the barred shape exactly as documented, in the app's existing "this X will not load" voice. The offer gate is a straight reactionsLeft comparison, correctly suppressing the option and correctly no-opping a press when reactionsLeft is 0.

AND reactionsLeft IS ALWAYS 0 FOR THE PLAYER, UNCONDITIONALLY, in this build -- not a new bug, named and dated in the app's own comment: "a reaction pool of zero, always -- PT-1534, nothing supplies a tier." Budgets construction hardcodes highestReactionTier: 0 as a literal, so whatever the player's Dex or BAB, the pool computes to zero regardless.

Tester built a fixture to confirm the zero-reaction suppression behaves correctly, which it does -- and named the other half as a scoped negative rather than working around it: it could not demonstrate the has-a-reaction case or the consumes-one-when-taken case, because no character build, feat, or state in the app can currently give the player a nonzero reactionsLeft. The confirmable half of the original ask is confirmed; the other half cannot currently be tested by anyone, not because the mechanism is wrong but because nothing feeds it.

RULED: this changes PT-1534 from a roadmap gap to a blocker. It was fine for a reaction pool to sit at zero while nothing consumed reactions -- now Interrupt is a shipped, tested-correct feature that no player can ever use, because nothing supplies the tier the gate reads. Whatever was going to supply highestReactionTier (Dex, BAB, a feat, a class table) needs to actually reach Budgets before Interrupt does anything for anyone.

## PT-1677 -- HUD BUILT: THE ROSTER IS A FOLD, THE PANEL JOINS TWO SOURCES ONCE, AND PT-1676 IS WITHDRAWN

The roster lives as a new projection, not an extension of PLAY-STATE-01, because it is transient by construction -- ENGINE-SPEC-04 writes no round to a save, so a roster restored from one would describe a fight that no longer exists. It folds a matched pair: an author's encounter.began (PT-1437, the kind alone is the effect, a request to start a fight) and the engine's own encounter.began, which the engine had never actually emitted -- _begin started fights and produced nothing to fold. Fixed: the engine's began carries subject and encounter, the same payload ended already carries, because a matched pair is the only shape a fold can close.

Membership (the fold) and the live numbers on each row (character.damaged, deliberately never logged, per projectPlayState's own note that lifetimes decide what is written in the first place) are two sources that can disagree, joined in exactly one place per PT-1468. The disagreement is itself a state a row can be in -- a member the round does not hold reads as still in the fight rather than vanishing or reading zero, because a bar at zero is nearly dead, a different and worse fact to get wrong by accident. hidden is told, not asked, from the same _concealed set Lens already uses -- no new event minted, per PT-1550.

Two defects found by cases that asked for something rather than merely ran: the dead colour was unreachable, because down/dying/dead are all at or below zero and the fill band the colour lives on has zero width in exactly those three states -- the track now carries the state when there is nothing left to fill. And the panel overflowed by 47px, caught by force_cast_test, a suite with nothing to do with the roster, because its window happened to be smaller.

PT-1675 CORRECTED: THE ZERO IS A FACT, NOT A STUB. ATTACKS-01 10 makes reaction uses the lower of the highest reaction tier and an ability allowance -- the allowance half is wired (Dex and BAB both reach Budgets), but the tier half has no source anywhere in the project. Its three reaction chains (Snap Shot, Overwatch, Parry) are not in base-rules -- no attacks.toml exists, Overwatch appears nowhere in the extract, CharacterRecord has no attacks field at all, and chargen has no step that would spend one. Zero is arithmetically correct for every character that can currently exist, and stays correct until attack rosters are extracted and a pick step is built -- not a wire to connect, a subsystem that does not exist yet.

WHAT THIS SLICE ACTUALLY CLOSED WAS THE SILENCE, not the zero: Beat.interrupts was empty for two different reasons -- this line offers none, and you cannot pay for the one it offers -- and a screen could not tell them apart. Beat.interruptsWithheld now says which, printing the reason rather than nothing. PT-1487's rule, one surface late. And both begin and choose dropped the new field on their first run, field-by-field reconstruction, despite a comment on the very field warning that a new one would be silently dropped -- a comment warning about a trap is not a guard against it.

PT-1676 WITHDRAWN. Coder read bundle/loom, the launcher stub, which does not change when Dart code changes -- the actual payload is kernel_blob.bin, and Coder rebuilt Loom's copy before reading its date, destroying the evidence. "Three days stale" is unestablished and the real cause of Tester's missing checkbox is unknown. Coder named this itself as its own artifact-versus-summary mistake and flagged the likely real cause for Tester to check: the grid's tap handler paints instead of selecting whenever a palette tool is armed, so an armed palette would hide the selection bar entirely.

TWO CHECKS REPAIRED: audit_rulings.py's heading regex accepted only an em dash, so PT-1670 onward (written with a double hyphen after an earlier syntax workaround) reported as cited-but-never-written and blocked the gate while sitting correctly in the file. All three dash forms are accepted now, on the reasoning that a check demanding one dash character from a human writing prose will go blind again. And check_event_producers caught its own stale allowance the hour the producer landed -- an exception that outlives its exception is permission nobody is using any more.

## PT-1678 -- HUD CONFIRMED LIVE, TWO SCOPED NEGATIVES, AND A REAL LIMIT SURFACED: EVERY FIGHT IN THIS BUILD IS 1-VS-1

Confirmed both halves live: player card and enemy row on screen from the first turn, bar fill widths shrinking in exact step with the combat log across five rounds, no lag or stale frame.

Hidden-combatant persistence and the dead/down/dying empty track are correct by code inspection and could not be observed in play, traced to why rather than left unresolved: Encounter's only constructor call site takes exactly two combatants. Every fight this build can construct is strictly 1-vs-1, so the instant either side reaches zero the fight ends and the roster panel closes in the same tick -- captured four frames at ~0.2-0.3s apart around a killing blow and the panel was already gone in all four. There is no third combatant to test hidden-persistence against and no visible window between alive-roster-open and dead-roster-closed in any fight the engine can currently build.

WORTH SURFACING DIRECTLY: PT-1672's whole design -- a roster that persists members through visibility changes, showing every combatant in the fight rather than filtering to visible ones -- is built and correct, and nothing has ever exercised the case it exists for, because the engine cannot currently construct a fight with more than two participants. The HUD is ready for multi-enemy combat; multi-enemy combat does not exist yet.

The checkbox mystery is half-solved, precisely: with a paint-type tool armed (terrain confirmed, and by the same unconditional-branch structure any paint variety), the tap handler intercepts unconditionally before occupancy is checked, hiding the selection bar on any square. Confirmed and reproduced. But a way-placement tool (doors) armed on an already-occupied square correctly falls back to selecting rather than attempting a duplicate placement -- a different code path, and Coder's hypothesis does not cover it. Named plainly as the one case that could not be reproduced rather than rounded up to solved: an already-placed doorway with the doorway tool itself armed.

A bonus confirmation: PT-1675's interrupt-withheld sentence, landed between sessions, produces the explicit "there is an interruption here and you have no reaction to spend" line -- a direct improvement on the exact gap TEST 054 filed, found by accident re-running an old fixture.

## PT-1679 -- CHECKBOX MYSTERY FULLY CLOSED. THE UNREPRODUCED CASE WAS A MISCLICK, AND THE REAL ANSWER IS A THIRD, DISTINCT BEHAVIOUR

Self-correction to TEST 055: the "doors armed" test had actually clicked the category header, which only expands to list doorway underneath -- nothing was armed, so the tap fell through to onSelect and looked like a normal selection. Testing "nothing armed" twice under a different label.

Re-run with the tool actually armed (category clicked to expand, then doorway clicked to arm -- confirmed by the text brightening, same tell as terrain/floor in 055): clicking an already-occupied door square opens the PlaceWayDialog itself, offering to place a SECOND connection on top of the first. Not a selection, not silence -- a third, distinct outcome, matching area_tab.dart's onPlaceWay callback exactly (no occupancy check anywhere in it). Confirmed it does not write until Place is pressed -- cancelled, diff clean, no selection bar shown at any point in the sequence.

None of the three is "hides the checkbox and does nothing else" -- the paint case remains the correct explanation for the original bug report (an author with a paint tool left armed from a prior action).

## PT-1680 -- MULTI-COMBATANT FIGHTS: THE ENGINE WAS NEVER THE LIMIT, ONE LIST LITERAL WAS. CORRECTS PT-1678

PT-1678 said Encounter's constructor takes exactly two combatants. It takes a List<Combatant> of any length -- every downstream piece (rollInitiative, beginRound/endRound, Encounter.standing, Fight.advance) already operated on the whole list. Encounter(combatants: [me, p.combatant]) in _begin was the only 1-vs-1 thing in the product, and the cause was one list literal at one call site, not the engine.

THE RULE ADDED: a creature already in contact with the fight is in it -- adjacent to the player or to whoever was touched, one hop, computed once, never a flood (a transitive walk would drag a corridor into a fight over a rule nobody has made). It invents nothing -- walking into something is already how a fight starts, so the old behaviour is this rule's one-enemy case.

NAMED CAREFULLY AS A READING, NOT A RULING ON THE BIGGER QUESTION: STUDY 31 6's real gap -- KOTOR engages automatically at 20m, ours at 0m -- is not what this closes. Detection at range would read PT-1573's range field and change how every package plays; this only says a creature already touching the fight is in it. Queued explicitly, not built: detection at range, faction-aware hostility (two enemies of different factions both join and both fight the player; FACTIONS-01 is not consulted in a fight), a hidden combatant staying hidden after striking, and initiative order still not shown.

TWO REAL DEFECTS SURFACED ONLY BY MULTI-ENEMY FIGHTS EXISTING:

A corpse stayed on its square and could be struck again mid-round. PT-1538 moved the dead-leave-the-board filter to two moments, arrival and end-of-fight, and in every 1-vs-1 fight so far the first death WAS the end of the fight, so both moments coincided and the gap between them was unreachable. character.died is written by _writeOutcome at fight end, so between a killing blow and the outcome the log could not yet say the body was gone, and the board-side fallen-set is log-derived. Fixed by joining fight-state and log-state in one place.

allies had been fed nothing: WhenAlone.shouldBreak reads v.allies.isEmpty, and enemyTurn built its target list as everyone-standing-except-me, correct in a 1-vs-1 and wrong the moment there are two enemies -- they would have shot each other, and a doctrine meant to break off when alone always broke off regardless of the actual roster, because the list it read was unconditionally empty. Fixed through Role/isParty, the same predicate the party-wipe rule already turns on, so there is one answer to "which side is this."

AND THREE TEST FIXTURES HAD BEEN RELYING ON A DEFAULT, ONE OF THEM ASSERTING THE WRONG SUBJECT ENTIRELY: Combatant.role defaults to player, and three test files built a trooper without ever stating a side. combatantFrom has passed role: Role.enemy for every real placement since PT-1515 -- the fixtures were wrong, not the code. One of them was worse: fight_test's dying-countdown cases bent the trooper into the negative band and watched it tick, but PT-1524 gives an enemy no dying band at all (dying and bleed appear zero times in KOTOR's whole API). The rule was right and the subject was a party member wearing an enemy's name -- only giving fights real sides made the mismatch visible. Corrected, with the enemy's no-band case added as the control alongside it.

A fixture Tester can use, built as a new package rather than an edit to any shared one (three other tests already walk endar-spire and a second creature adjacent to its own trooper would have joined their fights): two-enemies, two droids in contact plus a third hidden lurker above any passive detection this character can reach, all with enough vitality that the fight outlasts a blow and the bars move.

## PT-1681 -- TEST 055's CHECKBOX CASE: NOT LOW STAKES. A DUPLICATE DOORWAY WAS UNCATCHABLE BY EITHER PLAYER OR VALIDATOR

TEST 056 confirmed the way-placement dialog opens on an already-occupied square and does not write until Place is pressed, framing it as benign since nothing writes without confirmation. Coder actually pressed Place and checked what follows.

The cause was inverted: _tap returns unconditionally for every armed tool and never looks at what is already on the square -- the fallback-to-selection TEST 056 observed was Loom selecting hit.last, the SECOND doorway, not a refusal of the duplicate. Two doorways landed on one square, and the two halves of the product disagreed about which one existed: Loom's board editor only ever reaches the second (last-hit wins); the play screen's _step only ever takes the FIRST connection on a square; Lens draws both, identically, on top of each other. An author can only edit the one a player never uses, and deleting the one they can see leaves the working one untouched underneath it.

Verify said no problems found. PT-1379 -- the Builder must not be able to create a fault its own validator detects -- and no validator detected this one, so even a hand-edited file passed.

Fixed both ways, not just one: PackageProblem gains a member for it, and Loom refuses the placement AT THE TAP rather than waiting for Place -- PT-1500's own reasoning, a form built to be thrown away is not a form that works.

AND THE REFUSAL ITSELF WAS ALMOST UNREADABLE: it rode on the selection bar, which only renders when something is selected -- and a way-tool tap that hits an occupied square selects nothing. The project's own standing lesson pointed the other way (a dead-looking control is usually a refusal you did not read); a refusal nobody CAN read is the same defect with the blame relocated. Fixed alongside the rest.

## PT-1682 -- TURN ORDER BUILT, AND THE OWNER'S RISK WAS ONE LAYER UP FROM WHERE THE QUESTION WAS AIMED

The turn-order strip and rollInitiative's sort are the same list, not two things that could coincide -- Fight.order returns the object turn indexes into, and nextUp reads the same skip advance walks (built once, so a copy could not answer "whose turn next" differently than the fight itself does).

The owner's question -- confirm the display matches PT-1422's rule rather than matching the sort by coincidence -- had nothing to coincide at that layer, but the real risk was one layer up: a panel that independently re-sorted by initiative NUMBER would agree with the fight on every board where nobody ties, and only break on the first board where two do. Tested from both ends where each lives: fight_test proves a real tie (equal roll, equal Dexterity) resolves to ascending tag, not the order computed before the tie-break; roster_panel_test hands the strip pre-ordered numbers and requires it render them AS GIVEN, not re-sorted.

The proof that matters: a mutation replacing Fight.order with a stable sort by initiative alone changed nothing, because the list was already in that order -- the only way to make the two differ is to sort somewhere the rule is not. Reversing order fails both tie cases; sorting inside the panel fails the strip case. Recorded as the answer rather than treated as a fluke.

STRIKING REVEALS A HIDDEN COMBATANT, closing a case PT-1678's own multi-enemy fix opened: before multi-enemy fights, a hidden creature could not be pulled into a fight at all (contact both starts one and reveals). Adjacency-joining changed that, and a lurker could have fired every round from a square the board never drew. Fixed: only a strike reveals, not moving, not holding position, on the reasoning that what gives you away is the shot rather than the hit -- and the attacker is captured before the turn advances, since asking afterward would name whoever is up next rather than whoever just swung. The concealed-then-revealed window is real and stated as rarely directly observable (the fixture's synchronous first-enemy-turn collapses join and reveal into one call), proven instead by a mutation that fails with the lurker still marked concealed when the reveal is removed.

Self-correction: an assertion that pressing the turn-end key lands on whoever nextUp named was the wrong shape and was removed rather than weakened -- ending a turn runs the whole enemy half of the round, so the next combatant on screen is correctly the player again. nextUp versus advance belongs one layer down and is walked directly there, including the skip-a-fallen-combatant and null cases.

NOT DONE, NAMED: detection at range and faction-aware hostility remain queued design questions, not build tasks.


---

## PT-1683 -- A PARTY OF ONE GOING DOWN IS A WIPE. RULED AND NEVER SENT -- FOURTH INSTANCE, AND IT COST A REAL BUG

TEST 057: a dead player kept moving. The encounter never resolved -- one enemy correctly held for lack of a legal target, but the fight stayed open, position updated on arrow-key presses with no attack and no move-counter decrement, and the fallback read as an input path with no combat gate rather than intentional behaviour. Correctly identified by Tester as a symptom of a named gap rather than a surprise, and correctly not fixed by either agent -- the ruling was explicitly not theirs to make.

IT WAS MINE, AND I MADE IT WEEKS AGO IN A CODER PROMPT AND NEVER FILED IT TO THE LEDGER. "With a party of one, the player going down is a wipe. There is nobody left standing, and that is the loss condition." PT-1635 recorded the QUESTION (with a party of one, is the player going down a wipe?) but the answer given at the time never became a numbered ruling. Fourth instance of this corpus's own named failure mode -- an answer that exists in a chat message and not on record is an answer nobody can build against.

FORMALLY RULED NOW: PT-1633's wipe condition -- the whole party going down is the only permanent loss -- is satisfied when the party IS the player, today. A party of one has no "otherwise you're down and stand back up when the party wins" case, because there is no fight left to win. The encounter must resolve as a loss the moment the player crosses zero, exactly as a full-party wipe resolves under PT-1633, rather than continuing with an unkillable, unguarded body on the board.

Built as a fact about the party, not about the character -- it must read party-size, not "is this specific combatant the player," or it will be wrong the day a companion exists and the player alone going down is no longer the whole party.

## PT-1686 -- DETECTION AT RANGE: A CREATURE WITHIN ITS PERCEPTION RANGE JOINS ON CONTACT-PLUS-ONE ROUND. Owner sequencing, ruled to unblock Coder

Closing STUDY 31 6's gap. KOTOR engages automatically at 20m with a distance-scaled reaction delay (distance/10.0 seconds -- 2.0s at 20m default, 0.5s at 5m, the creature turning to face at half the delay before it acts). PT-1496 governs which half transfers: the trigger transfers, the real-time delay arithmetic does not, because we have no seconds, only rounds.

THE DISTANCE IS ALREADY RULED, REUSED RATHER THAN INVENTED: PT-1571 settled one default perception range with no per-species or per-chassis table, ten squares (20m), matching 97.8% of 4,397 KOTOR blueprints. That same number is the detection radius. No new field, no new ruling on the distance itself.

THE DELAY PORTS AS A ROUND, NOT A FRACTION OF ONE. KOTOR runs 3-second rounds (ACTION-ECONOMY-01 167); at the maximum detection distance the source delay is 2.0 seconds -- under one round. A creature detected at any distance within its own range reacts within a single round in the source material, so the honest port is a flat one-round delay, not a distance-scaled one: finer granularity than "under one round" does not exist on our clock.

RULED: a creature within perception range of the player joins the fight (per PT-1678's roster) the round it is detected, but does not act until the round after -- present, visible, marked not-yet-acting, the turn-based equivalent of KOTOR's visible turn-to-face before the swing. This is an EXTENSION of PT-1678's contact rule, not a replacement: adjacency still joins a creature immediately with no delay, because contact is not detection at range, it is already touching. The delay applies only to a creature pulled in purely by distance.

Hidden creatures are unaffected -- PT-1550's contact-is-the-reveal floor and PT-1682's strike-reveals rule both stand; detection at range finds an UNHIDDEN creature that was simply too far away to have joined yet, not a concealed one.

## PT-1687 -- FACTION-AWARE HOSTILITY: A CREATURE JOINS ON CONTACT OR RANGE ONLY IF ITS FACTION STARTS HOSTILE TO THE PLAYER'S

FACTIONS-01 4b is already the exact specification and has been settled since PT-670: "a faction declaration says who starts hostile. What happens after is the GM's and the package's." Not a reputation track -- INFLUENCE-01 owns earned standing and it is for companions, not for whether a stranger attacks on sight. A faction is a property of the campaign (PT-680/685), not of the character, and both shipped packages already declare one.

THE GAP PT-1680 NAMED: nothing decides who is hostile beyond contact and a conversation, so two creatures of different factions standing adjacent to each other both currently join a fight and both attack the player, regardless of what either faction actually is.

RULED: PT-1678's contact rule and PT-1686's range rule both gain one precondition -- a creature joins the fight only if its declared faction is hostile to the player's, per the campaign's FACTIONS-01 declaration. A creature whose faction is not hostile does not join on contact or range; it stands there, uninvolved, exactly as 4b already promises for anything the package has not separately scripted hostile.

This does not touch what happens once two creatures are already fighting each other for unrelated reasons (a scripted encounter, a conversation gone wrong) -- 4b's "what happens after is the GM's and the package's" leaves that to authored content, not to this check. The gate is only at the moment of joining by contact or range.

## PT-1688 -- TWO FIXTURES PREPPED AGAINST CODER'S MID-EDIT CODE, AND A QUESTION WORTH RAISING WHEN THE BUILD LANDS

Tester read Coder's actual uncommitted implementation before building rather than guessing from the ruling text alone, and found something PT-1686 left ambiguous: _detectAtRange early-returns when no fight is active, so as written it only pulls a latecomer into an ALREADY-STARTED fight from range. STUDY 31's own source finding was that perception-at-range is how KOTOR STARTS combat in the first place (k_def_percept01 gates a fresh engagement, not just a reinforcement) -- so whether an idle, undetected hostile enemy should be able to initiate a fight purely from a player walking within range, with no fight yet running, is a real question PT-1686's wording did not settle either way.

The ranged-detection fixture (package "ranged-detection", a 16x3 corridor with full line of sight, a contact-adjacent starter guard at distance 1 and a second guard at distance 12) is built to test both readings directly: engaging the starter then closing distance tests the latecomer case Coder's code currently supports; bypassing the starter and approaching the distant guard cold tests whether range alone, with nothing already fighting, does anything -- which the current code says it should not.

Not a defect to fix yet, since the build is mid-edit. Worth asking directly when Coder reports: does perception at range only reinforce an existing fight, or should it also be able to start one? If the latter, the corridor fixture is deliberately shaped to prove it.

The mixed-faction fixture (package "mixed-faction", declared Republic; a Sith Raider and a Republic Trooper both adjacent to the entry and to each other) confirmed one thing worth recording as intentional rather than a gap: walking directly into a creature bypasses the faction gate entirely and always engages via the existing talk-or-fight logic, regardless of that creature's faction. PT-1687's gate was scoped to whether OTHER creatures join by contact or range, not to the primary creature a player walks directly into -- confirmed in source as deliberate. Correctly read; no correction needed.

Both fixtures verify clean in Loom, no package touched outside the two new ones, both Loom instances launched and killed by PID with Coder's own instance confirmed untouched throughout.

PT-1686 reused PT-1571's already-settled default range and the round-delay math held exactly as derived -- every distance inside a 20m detection radius reacts within one round against a 3-second round, so the port is a flat one-round mark rather than any arithmetic. ## PT-1690 -- CORRECTS PT-1687: THE PREMISE WAS FALSE, CHECKED AND CAUGHT BEFORE BUILDING AGAINST IT

PT-1687 asserted faction was "a static campaign-level fact already on every shipped package." Checked before building, and it was not true of any of them: zero of seven packages on the shelf declared a faction, zero creature blueprints declared one, and PACKAGE-FORMAT-01 had no field for it at all. The character-level reader has existed since AUTHORED-CHARACTER-01 2a with nothing anywhere ever filling it in.

Built the actual gap rather than the false premise: [package] faction added to the format. startsHostile returns three states, not two, because reading absence as not-hostile would mean nothing could ever attack a player again -- undeclared joins, absence-versus-error in the one place where getting it wrong empties the game of its own combat.

The hostility rule itself -- same faction is peace, different faction is war -- is explicitly labelled a READING rather than a ruling, because FACTIONS-01 gives factions, nesting, and 4b's sentence, but no hostility matrix. Its own known hole is named and pinned rather than silently accepted: 2ab makes the Jedi Order a subfaction of the Republic, so a Jedi should read as not-hostile to a Republic soldier, and this reading compares faction names directly, so it currently says they are hostile. The nesting tree exists only as prose in FACTIONS-01 and is in no extract, so implementing it correctly would mean extracting the tree first. A test is pinned to fail the day that extraction lands, so the hole cannot go unnoticed once the data exists to close it.

check_fenced_examples caught its own author mid-mistake: the new faction section had been inserted inside PACKAGE-FORMAT-01's manifest worked example rather than beside it -- exactly PT-1495's family, a worked example is what an author copies, caught before it shipped wrong.

Three shelf-count tests went red from the environment growing (four packages to seven, as Tester published the two new fixtures for these exact rulings), attributed correctly rather than treated as this slice's fault, and fixed at the root: a horizontally-scrolling library ListView only builds what is on screen, so find.text checks had been silently measuring "does this tile fit at 1280 pixels" rather than "is this package present." Rewritten to check the row's actual contents against what each package declares.

## PT-1691 -- LINE OF SIGHT BUILT FOR DETECTION AT RANGE. A CREATURE COULD SEE THROUGH SOLID ROCK, AND A SECOND BUG WAS FOUND ONLY BY LOOKING FOR A THIRD

TileType.blocksSight has existed since the format was written and was read by nothing -- PT-1550's own note recorded that as deliberate, since hidden is an author's flag rather than a perception system. PT-1686 made the absence a real defect: detection compared distance alone, so a creature noticed the player through solid rock at any range under the radius.

Built symmetric by construction rather than as a single directional walk, because a single Bresenham line is not symmetric -- some diagonal pairs clear A-to-B and block B-to-A, which would mean the player could be detected from a square the detecting creature could not itself be seen from. A line is clear when either traversal is; swept across all 625 ordered pairs on a test board rather than spot-checked, because the asymmetric pairs are exactly what a hand-picked example misses. Endpoints are never asked about a wall standing in the origin or target square does not blind or hide anything standing on it, which is an off-by-one, not a sight rule.

A SECOND, INDEPENDENT BUG FOUND WHILE LOOKING FOR A THIRD: detection was never evaluated at the moment a fight begins, only on subsequent steps -- because a step that walks INTO a creature returns before the step's own detection call runs. A creature already standing in range when a fight started went undetected until somebody moved afterward, a full round late if the player won initiative. It survived every existing test because the enemy-turn loop also runs detection, and in every fixture that could start a fight the enemy won initiative -- the gap was invisible for exactly the fights the tests were able to construct.

range CAME OUT FROM BEHIND hidden, correctly generalized: it existed only for PT-1573's find-on-approach (which only ever asks about a hiding creature), and PT-1686 gave it a second reader that asks about UNHIDDEN creatures -- so hidden-only stopped being a rule and became an accidental limitation. One number, read from whichever side is deciding: how far off something can be noticed and how far off it notices are the same distance. stealth itself correctly stays hidden-only, since a hiding total on something in plain sight is two contradictory statements. Loom's authoring control was updated in the same pass, or the fix would have inverted PT-1379 -- an author unable to write something the reader now accepts.

Self-caught: PT-1691 was minted and written through code, tests and documentation before audit_rulings.py blocked the gate on "cited but never written," per PT-1508's rule that numbers are the owner's to assign. Corrected to cite PT-1686, whose gap this closes, with the follow-up named as the owner's to number. The same check repaired two slices ago for going blind to a dash character caught its own author minting a number this time.

NAMED, NOT FIXED, CORRECTLY STOPPING AT THE EDGE OF AUTHORITY: find-on-approach (PT-1573, a hidden creature noticing the player) has the identical defect -- it compares distance with no line of sight, so a hidden creature can still be found through a solid wall. Not fixed, because it is a RULED behaviour and this slice had no ruling authorizing the change. Also named: ranged attacks do not consult sight either (PT-1543's bands are pure distance, so a wall does not block a shot), faction nesting stays blocked on extraction, and a creature that loses sight mid-fight correctly stays in the roster per STUDY 32's deliberate do-not-make-visibility-the-membership-rule finding.

## PT-1694 -- RANGED ATTACKS ALSO NEED LINE OF SIGHT. Extends the same canSee check to PT-1543's range bands

Coder named it: a ranged attack currently checks only distance, so a wall blocks nothing -- a player or enemy can shoot straight through solid rock at anything within range. ## PT-1695 -- PT-1694 BUILT, AND IT CONSOLIDATED A SECOND COPY THE COMMENT HAD ALREADY DENIED EXISTED

Three callers now share one sight check -- detection, find-on-approach, and a ranged attack -- where the comment governing this code had claimed one answer for three callers while the code actually held two: detection had built its own inline canSee call rather than sharing it. Fixed to route through the one shared function, closing "a creature detectable through a wall it could not be shot through" before it could exist as a live inconsistency.

RULED, THE OWNER'S OPEN CHOICE: a shot filters its candidate list rather than refusing an already-chosen target. Refusing wastes the turn -- a doctrine that picks an unseeable target and is then told no has spent its Action on something that was never possible, with the player watching a creature do nothing and no explanation given. Enemy targeting is already filtered by side; sight is one more clause in the same filter, and decide stays grid-free as DOCTRINE-FORMAT-01 requires. A creature with nothing visible holds, and says so. Contact stays exempt everywhere -- touching squares always see each other, nothing between them to ask about.

PT-1692's find-on-approach settled correctly on a genuine subtlety: "settled" means asked-and-answered, and a wall is not an answer. The passive take-10 is taken once and stands -- re-asking would just repeat the same number -- but a wall blocking the check is not a number to settle on. Stepping into a sightline for the first time takes the passive then, for the first time, rather than treating "behind a wall" as a permanent hiding place the mechanic was never meant to grant.

SELF-CAUGHT: the sees parameter was optional, null meaning "this caller has no walls" -- coherent on its face, since every test bed is an open field. A mutation removing sees: from the one real caller passed the entire suite anyway, meaning the one caller that mattered could silently stop asking and nothing anywhere would notice. Made required, on the same reasoning PT-1593 already established for squaresApart on this identical method: a bed with no walls says so in one line; a caller that forgot cannot, and forgetting is now a compile error rather than a silent pass.

NOT DONE, NAMED: an enemy that loses its line holds rather than repositioning toward cover -- unruled AI behaviour, and the honest floor is simply that it does not shoot through rock. Force powers do not yet consult sight at all (power_target.dart picks by distance alone, the same shape a shot had before this slice) -- named as the next instance of this exact pattern rather than built now, since it belongs to PT-1488's own surface.

## PT-1699 -- AN UNRECOGNIZED STEP NAME IN discards FALLS BACK TO DISCARDING EVERYTHING AFTER IT, LOUDLY. Owner ruling, closes PT-1698's open question

clear's switch has no default, so a step name it does not recognise is silently ignored on replay -- the exact failure the discard list exists to prevent, invisible.

RULED: an unrecognized name discards everything after it, the same way an explicit step-reopen already does -- reusing existing machinery rather than inventing new handling. Reasoning: if the current build does not recognise a step, it cannot know what that step did or what later steps depended on, so the safe assumption is that nothing forward of it can be trusted.

NOT silent, and NOT a refusal to load. This is PT-1526's shape, applied a second time: do not lock the player out of a save over it, and do not pretend nothing happened. The load succeeds, the fallback is visible somewhere discoverable -- a log line or a fault a future check can catch -- even though it need not block the character screen or reach the player directly. Refusing to load was rejected as the harshest option for the rarest failure (a renamed or removed step); silently keeping the data was rejected as defeating the whole purpose of the discard list, since the warning would only ever reach a developer, never the player it's protecting.

## PT-1700 -- TEST 059: LINE OF SIGHT AND IMMEDIATE DETECTION BOTH CONFIRMED, AND A SELF-CORRECTION THAT CAUGHT ITS OWN BRIEF GOING STALE MID-SESSION

Three fixtures, three confirmations.

Line of sight gates _detectAtRange, not just range: a guard 9 squares out behind a full wall held for two full rounds despite being in range the whole time, joined immediately the instant the player crossed past the wall -- confirmed it's sight gating the join, resuming exactly where the line opens, with the same notice-then-act-next-round delay TEST 058 already confirmed.

Immediate detection confirmed even when the player wins initiative: a DEX-18 build topped the turn order at 16, and in the same first frame -- before any action -- a second guard 6 squares away in the clear was already in the roster marked noticing. This is exactly the case PT-1683's own fix comment named as what the old bug needed to manifest, and ending the turn confirmed the second half: the reinforcement took its real turn at the round boundary, detected on arrival rather than a round late, still correctly held to its own skip.

AND A SELF-CORRECTION REPORTED PLAINLY: the fixture was built to confirm a real, then-current gap (canSee existed only on the ranged-attack path, not the find), and by the time it was actually played, PT-1692+PT-1694 had landed mid-session and closed exactly that gap -- confirmed structurally rather than assumed, including that a wrong not-found never freezes permanently (re-approaching from a fresh angle worked without needing a second character).

Two things named rather than chased: whether the reinforcement path settles behind a wall the same way an ordinary find does, and canSee's own documented diagonal-corner permissiveness -- neither tested this session.

## PT-1702 -- PT-1675 CORRECTED: THE TIER WAS NEVER THE POOL'S GATE. NO ATTACK ROSTER WAS EVER NEEDED, AND EVERY CHARACTER IN THE PRODUCT WAS THE ONE NAMED CASE WHERE ZERO IS RIGHT

PT-1675 and PT-1677 both framed the reaction-tier gap as a missing subsystem -- no attacks.toml, no attacks field, no pick step, treated as the reason Interrupt stayed unreachable. That framing is wrong, and not from ambiguity: reactionPool computed min(allowance, tier), which is ATTACKS-01 10 read as the pool's gate. 12.7 of the SAME document exists to say that reading is wrong -- "10's lower of tier and allowance caps how many times a CHAIN may fire. It does not gate the pool itself. Opportunity attacks are universal." ACTION-ECONOMY-01 10 says it from the other side: universal, drawing on the reaction pool, no chain applies.

Both documents name the same character for the zero-reaction case, and it is +0 Dexterity and +0 base attack bonus, not "holds no chain": a Consular, and it reads correctly. With the chain cap wrongly placed inside the pool computation and no chain acquirable anywhere, every character in the product was, arithmetically, the one named case where zero is the right answer. That is what kept Interrupt built, tested and unreachable for eleven slices -- not a missing subsystem, a formula reading one document's local rule as a global gate.

NOT A RULING -- the reconciling text is the document itself, naming 10 explicitly and unambiguous once read. What was missing was that anything had read it. The chains themselves (Parry, Snap Shot, Overwatch) are still unbuilt and are now correctly a content gap rather than a blocker -- 10's cap arrives with the first chain, since a cap with nothing to apply it to would be declared and read by nothing.

PT-1699 CONFIRMED BUILT. clear reports an unknown step name now rather than silently ignoring it, falling back through the same mechanism an explicit reopen uses. "Everything after it" has no smaller safe bound, and the reason is exact: the list is ordered, so a bound from that order would be free, but a RENAMED step sits earlier than the names that follow it -- an unplaceable name has no position, so everything is forward of it. ReplayOutcome.unknownDiscards is the fault a future check can catch; nothing consumes it yet, and the field says so rather than pretending otherwise. CHARACTER-RECORD-01's section was stale in both halves it claimed ("six fields today" and "nothing has ruled what it writes") -- corrected, clear handles nine steps.

PT-1701 CORRECTED: THE BUILD WAS NEVER BROKEN BY TWO DISAGREEING COMMITS. Measured at the two heads: Lodestar's signature has no tier parameter, the app's own committed pubspec.lock names that same commit, package_config.json resolves to it, and the build compiles clean. The pushed history was never inconsistent.

THE REAL CAUSE IS A THIRD ARTIFACT NEITHER THE LOCK NOR THE HEAD COMPARISON CAN SEE: .dart_tool/package_config.json, generated, gitignored, per-checkout. Tester and Coder share one working tree. Mid-slice, that tree can hold an edited source file against a not-yet-repinned lock -- producing exactly the observed error, from a tree where git status looks like ordinary work in progress. Coder hit the identical error independently this same slice. No pair of PUSHED commits produces it; only the uncommitted middle of a shared tree does.

"The lock matches HEAD" is two of three artifacts that decide what a build actually runs. The third is the one a shared working tree breaks first, and nothing in the current tooling serialises one agent's slice against another agent editing the same tree. Named rather than invented around. Tester stopping rather than patching past it remains the right call -- the diagnosis of WHY was incomplete, the decision to hold was not.

## PT-1703 -- ONCE ADMITTED TO COMBAT, A COMBATANT STAYS -- CONFIRMED AS INTENDED, NOT A GAP. Tester found it, declined to rule on it, this closes it

TEST 060: built a fixture specifically to get a guard to join mid-fight then go fully out of sight afterward, not just before joining. It stayed in the roster unchanged for two more rounds. Read the reason before concluding empirically: _detectAtRange's loop skips anyone already in encounter.combatants unconditionally -- there is no un-admit path anywhere in the code. Correctly declined to rule on whether this is intended or a gap, reporting the mechanism only.

RULED: intended, and it is not a new decision -- PT-1672 already made this call from the other direction. "A combatant that goes out of sight is NOT removed from the panel -- the row stays, marked hidden" was about display, but the reasoning under it is about membership: STUDY 32 found BG3 keeps a roster where you can fight what you cannot see, and it does not un-admit on lost sight either -- membership persists until an explicit leave. STUDY 31 found KOTOR DOES un-join on lost sight, and PT-1672 explicitly chose the BG3 shape because we are turn-based and KOTOR's real-time disengage-on-lost-sight was named as the wrong model to port to a grid.

So this is that same choice, one layer down from where it was first made: admission is the permanent record, sight-independent from that moment, and the only way out of a fight is for the fight to end -- not for a combatant to slip out of it by breaking line of sight. Filed explicitly so it is not later "fixed" as a bug report against a design already ruled.

Also confirmed this session: the diagonal-corner exploit is real rather than a docstring claim -- canSee's algorithm was copied into a throwaway script, a checkerboard corner computed, and the model matched exact squares in play, not approximately. And PT-1699's discard cascade confirmed for the only case live play can produce (re-opening an earlier chargen step); the actual unknown-step-name fallback needs a hand-crafted save no ordinary player's file would produce, and Tester correctly declined to fabricate one to force it.

A FOURTH ARTIFACT NAMED, independently: package_config.json, gitignored, per-checkout, goes stale in a tree two agents edit at once -- confirms PT-1702's finding, declared by Tester on its own account after hitting the identical build failure before reading the correction.

## PT-1704 -- OPPORTUNITY ATTACKS BUILT, DISENGAGE SHIPPED WITH THEM AS ITS ONLY PREVENTER

ACTION-ECONOMY-01 10 chosen because it waits on nothing: no chain applies, so it is the one reaction not blocked by the still-unbuilt attack rosters (Parry, Snap Shot, Overwatch). PT-1675's pool fix made it buildable the day it landed.

Reach is inside the threatened square, was <= reach, because the square you can be hit from is the square you are threatened in -- and it is what gives a reach weapon its entire value. Closing provokes nothing, deliberately, pinned separately from the general distance-changed case because a symmetric test would pass every other case and invert this one. The blow lands at the STARTING distance, the opposite of enemyTurn's choice and not an inconsistency -- enemyTurn measures where a mover ended because it moved and then swung; this fires because the mover left, so at the ending distance they are already out of reach by definition and the rule could never fire if it read that number. A watcher strikes unarmed rather than with a blaster, reusing the codebase's existing word for no-melee-weapon rather than inventing a pistol-whip.

Droids make none -- present.kind already answers is-this-a-droid since PT-1490, reused rather than a second notion invented, and applies to a droid PLAYER too, not just enemies. Printed the mirror of an already-found defect (five reaction uses across four droids, none spendable) rather than building a new instance of it.

Disengage shipped in the same commit as its own trigger, on the reasoning that a rule built without its only named counter is one that can only ever be suffered -- the twin of "an exception that outlives its exception," a rule that arrives without its own. Set-then-pay on the Action spend, because set-then-succeed would be a free Disengage that deletes 10 rather than countering it. Dies at next startTurn per 1's "YOUR movement" reading. First Action in the product that is not Attack.

TWO DEFECTS FOUND BY CASES ASKING FOR SOMETHING: the reaction pip could not show a spend, because left and total were drawn from the same field, so a spent reaction showed as one fewer star with nothing to compare against -- could not be wrong until now, since nothing outside a conversation had ever spent one. Same shape as PT-1540's spent-pip-goes-grey being unreachable for the Action. And one of Coder's own tests was vacuous: "an ally leaving reach provokes nothing" passed under a mutation that deletes the side check too, because the fixture's zero-pool trooper made affordability the real reason it passed, not sides. Rebuilt with a control of identical geometry differing only in side; the mutation fails now.

NOT DONE, NAMED: the enemy half is wired and cannot fire on any board that exists, because enemyTurn only ever closes on its one possible target and the party is one -- wired anyway so the rule is not forgotten onto the second path the day a companion exists, worth a TEST pass then, not before. Path is not read (two endpoints only; exact for the player's one-square step, not for approach's multi-square walk). Forced movement and reach weapons both named as future callers of the same check rather than special-cased. Ready remains unused with zero real uses across six scenarios -- a discoverability problem, not a rules gap, per its own prior note.

## PT-1705 -- THE EIGHT BOOKS, IDENTITY-FIRST. Owner ruling, closes AUTHOR's WALL at 3 (the chapter-numbering collision) and settles what OUTLINE-01 could not

AUTHOR's first deliverable jumped to chapter lists before book identity existed. The owner paused it and settled identity one book at a time, in conversation, before any further outlining. This is that settlement.

EIGHT BOOKS. FIVE CORE, THREE SUPPLEMENTARY.

CORE -- what a table needs to play a session:

1. PLAYER'S HANDBOOK. Build and run a character: standard classes (13) + Force classes (6), skills, feats, action economy and combat, death and difficulty, the Force (pool/powers/forms), alignment, character record, starting equipment for buying, pregens. AND PLAYABLE SPECIES, folded back in as its own chapter -- this is the decision that resolves AUTHOR's WALL 1 collision. SPECIES-CHAPTER-v2 and CLASSES-STANDARD-PHB were already drafted as chapters of one single-PHB spine; this ruling returns to that spine rather than fighting it. Less work than pulling species out, not more -- the existing prose mostly fits as-is.

2. GAMEMASTER'S HOLOCRON. The GM's toolkit: setting DCs, influence, factions, awarding XP, encounter design, playtest scenarios. Table-facing, not player-facing.

3. GALACTIC THREAT DATABASE. Everything hostile, one book: humanoid adversaries, droid opponents, hostile beasts. Not "humanoid and droid" -- BEASTS ARE IN THIS BOOK TOO, ruled explicitly below. In-universe framing intended (a Republic/guild-maintained registry), same trick as Holocron's own naming.

4. PLANETARY ATLAS. The gazetteer. MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED: data/extracted/worlds.json holds 301 world entries, not the 290 first floated in conversation -- corrected before it became the working number. This is not a thin book. At 301 entries it is a full reference volume on its own, which is why it stayed separate from Timeline rather than merging into it (see below) and why it earned core status on size and necessity both -- Star Wars is its planets the way D&D generally is not.

5. GALACTIC TIMELINE. The dated spine: eras, major events, where Revan and the Sith Wars sit on the clock. Kept separate from Atlas rather than merged -- a 301-entry gazetteer plus a full history is two different reading modes (look-up versus sequence), and cramming both into one spine would recreate the single-oversized-book problem the Bestiary cut was meant to avoid. LINKED RATHER THAN MERGED: timeline entries may reference world names ("the Battle of X happened on [World]") as a cheap cross-reference instead of a structural fusion.

SUPPLEMENTARY -- adds depth, a table can run without these on day one:

6. SPECIES COMPENDIUM. NOT a chargen book any more -- that content moved to the PHB. This is now the alien encyclopedia: all species of the Old Republic, playable and non-playable both, not gated to character options. Old Republic overview chapter retained. BEASTS GET AN ENTRY HERE TOO, split by function from their Threat Database stat block and their Advanced Player's Guide ownership rules -- same creature, three jobs, same pattern droids already use (see below). This book answers "what is a wompa," the Threat Database answers "how do I fight one," the APG answers "how do I tame one."

7. ARMORY. Weapons, armor, gear, upgrades, droid construction/upgrade, starships. The PHB's own starting-equipment précis covers day-one buying; this is the full catalog and does not block play.

8. ADVANCED PLAYER'S GUIDE. Prestige classes, deeper multiclassing, and BEAST OWNERSHIP MECHANICS specifically -- obedience DCs, upkeep, the Beast Master class, "beasts a player can take." Explicitly the "unlocks after you've played" book, not core by its own definition.

THE BESTIARY IS CUT. Everything it would have held is either combat data (now Galactic Threat Database) or ownership mechanics (now Advanced Player's Guide) or lore (now Species Compendium). No content lost; no book left with nothing of its own to say.

DROIDS SPLIT THREE WAYS BY FUNCTION, THE PATTERN BEASTS NOW FOLLOW TOO: Species Compendium carries the playable/lore half (seven chassis, droid skills, playing one as a character), Galactic Threat Database carries the combat stat block, Armory carries construction and upgrade (ITEMS-04's 135 droid items already live there). A droid is three different things depending on which question is being asked -- play it, fight it, or build it -- and the book split follows the question, not the noun.

STOP-REPORT ITEM STILL OPEN, NOT SETTLED HERE: AUTHOR's WALL 2 (the source books are not staged into HANDOFF and AUTHOR cannot read them to cite folio-and-line) is unrelated to identity and remains for Coder to stage.

## PT-1706 -- BUILD 133: PT-1637 AND PT-1645 BOTH FIXED. Coder read all eight of its own unread rulings and closed three

PT-1637: approach() was a greedy Chebyshev descent that could strand a creature with nowhere legal to go -- every nearer neighbour wall, the open ones all sideways. Coder's own earlier comment argued against fixing it ("inventing A* would be inventing a rule about what a creature knows"), and it named the flaw in its own argument: greedy descent was equally an invention, with no more support in the corpus and the added property of looking like a bug. Fixed with a uniform-cost search bounded by the creature's own movement points this turn -- §1's speed is the horizon, so no perception rule gets invented, and costs rather than step-count so PT-1513's difficult-ground doubling is respected rather than routed around blindly. On open ground the cheapest route is still the straight line with the same tie-breaks, so every previously-working board is unaffected -- the change is confined to the boards PT-1637 actually filed.

TWO OF CODER'S OWN TESTS WERE WRONG BEFORE THE CODE WAS: the first pillar board had a free diagonal route around a three-deep wall, so the broken mutation passed the headline test; rebuilt on PT-1637's actual board where every nearer neighbour is wall. And a detour test asserted its own premise wrong -- expected the route around a short wall to be longer than straight-line and it is exactly the same length; the test was wrong, not the walk. A third case hung rather than failed (an awaited file write inside testWidgets never completes) -- written synchronously now, cause named in the file.

PT-1645: the header row read a frozen field; PT-1641 had already located why (_entry assigned only on open/New Game/hub-play, never during play). Now reads the same ledger expression Continue and Load already use, not a second opinion -- reverting the fix reproduces PT-1639's exact sentence. AND a second defect found by measuring rather than reasoning: fixing the Expanded/Flexible imbalance was only half the fix, because with the halves no longer competing the detail wants more width than the panel's fixed size gives it -- what was being silently lost was the UNIT (7 ho / 19 ho / 14 with nothing after it). Two-line fix once measured.

THREE REAL QUESTIONS SURFACED, NAMED RATHER THAN GUESSED AT:

PT-1638 -- diagonal keys do nothing, and it strands a player (an arrival with all four orthogonals blocked, two diagonals open floor, no fight-free way out). The rule is settled (PT-1588), only the keyboard is missing four bindings. Coder asked which four before building.

PT-1640 -- species reaches speed and not ability scores off the same blueprint field; whether a blueprint's species should also carry ability adjustments is a rules question, named rather than assumed.

PT-1653 -- Console Home cannot distinguish a clean package from a broken one; first sign of trouble is a warning band inside a room already entered. A design question, not a build question.

## PT-1707 -- DIAGONAL MOVEMENT BINDS TO NUMPAD 7/9/1/3. Owner ruling, answers Coder's "say the word" on PT-1638

RULED: numpad 7, 9, 1, 3 for northwest/northeast/southwest/southeast, alongside the existing four arrow keys for the orthogonals. Standard roguelike numpad convention -- the compass layout (7 8 9 / 4 . 6 / 1 2 3) is the one a player is most likely to already carry from other games in this genre, and it needs no relearning once the orthogonal arrows are already known.

Scope: this is the immediate fix for the stranding case PT-1638 names (an arrival boxed in on all four orthogonals with open diagonal floor), not a substitute for PT-1443's click-to-move. Both stand -- click-to-move remains the eventual general answer; four numpad keys close the specific player-facing bug now rather than waiting on a larger feature.

## PT-1708 -- OPPORTUNITY ATTACKS NEVER FIRE IN PLAY, REPRODUCIBLY. The engine test proves clause composition and nothing about the app's wiring

BUILD 132 shipped ACTION-ECONOMY-01 10. Tester confirmed the ordinary pieces work: the guard's own Strike fires correctly, Disengage spends the Action and prints its line correctly, the droid's own ordinary Strike also fires (flagged separately, unchased -- whether melee-closed-to-droids is scoped to opportunity attacks only or is a wider unenforced rule elsewhere).

THE TRIGGER ITSELF NEVER FIRED. Confirmed three separate times against an organic guard -- cold, after re-approaching, after pressing Disengage first -- stepping from distance 1 to distance 2, the exact leavesReach condition. No strike, no log line, no damage, ever.

TRACED BEFORE CONCLUDING, NOT ASSUMED: leavesReach's own math checks out (1 to 2 across reach 1). The guard's reaction pool computes to 1 via reactionPool(dexModifier: 0, baseAttackBonus: 1) -- not zero, so PT-1675's fix reaches this creature. The corridor has no walls, so canSee has nothing to refuse against. Sides are plainly hostile -- the same guard is already landing ordinary Strikes. The before/after snapshot ordering matches what the source says it should. Everything readable from outside the running process says this should fire, and it did not.

ITS OWN DIAGNOSIS, STATED AS A READ RATHER THAN A GUESS: Coder's opportunity_attack_test.dart almost certainly calls Fight.opportunityAttacks directly with hand-built callbacks -- which proves the engine's clause composition and proves nothing about the app's own _step/_reachSnapshot/_opportunities wiring, exactly the seam a real playthrough exercises and an engine-level unit test does not. The droid half is unconfirmable as correctly-excluded given the base case already fails for a guard with every reason to swing.

CORRECTLY STOPPED SHORT OF DIAGNOSING TO A PATCH: traced every external input and did not instrument the running app to find the exact failing line, naming that as the boundary between confirming and fixing rather than crossing it.

## PT-1709 -- NO DIAGONAL CORNER-CUTTING, FOR SIGHT AND MOVEMENT BOTH. Owner ruling, matches D&D 3.5's Line of Effect rule and closes a disagreement between canSee and PT-1707's new keys

D&D 3.5's Line of Effect rule: sight, targeting and effects cannot be drawn diagonally through the point where two walls touch only at their corner -- a diagonal pinch is not an opening, even though the destination square past it may be open. Movement is not stated as explicitly in the core rules but is the standard table extension of the same logic, and it is the one this project adopts: if a corner blocks an arrow, it blocks a person.

RULED: neither sight nor diagonal movement may cross a corner where both flanking orthogonal squares are blocked. A diagonal step (or a diagonal line of sight) is only legal when at least one of the two squares it cuts between is open.

THIS CLOSES A REAL DISAGREEMENT ALREADY ON RECORD, NOT A HYPOTHETICAL ONE. PT-1703 confirmed canSee's own documented behaviour is the opposite -- two walls meeting at a diagonal do NOT seal the gap in the current implementation, verified exploitable in play (TEST 060's corner-peek fixture). PT-1707's new diagonal movement keys would inherit that same permissiveness on the movement side if built against the current canSee logic unchanged. Both need the corner check; building movement without it would ship a second copy of a defect already found and named on the sight side.

Scope: applies to sight (canSee), diagonal movement (the new numpad keys), and by the same reasoning anything else that reads canSee or its geometry going forward -- ranged attacks, the find-on-approach check, and any future power or ability that draws a line. One shared geometry check, not a rule re-derived per caller.

## PT-1712 -- PT-1709 BUILT: diagonalIsOpen, ONE FUNCTION, THREE CALLERS, TERRAIN NOT PASSABILITY

canSee's own comment had defended the leak in its own words -- "two walls meeting at a diagonal do not seal the diagonal, which is what a player looking at the board expects." Fixed as one shared function (sight, approach, the player's step), exactly the shape asked for rather than three rules that could drift.

Asks TERRAIN, not passability, deliberately: an occupied square is not a wall, so two creatures standing diagonally do not wall each other in, which no rule ever said they should. approach takes a separate blocksCorner flag for the cases that do care, defaulting to passable so every existing bed is unchanged.

TWO NARROWINGS PUT ON THE RECORD RATHER THAN LEFT IMPLICIT: contact is no longer unconditionally exempt from the check everywhere -- PLAY-STATE-01's "touching squares always see each other, there is nothing between them to ask about" stops being true when both flanks are wall; orthogonal contact is untouched, each half has its own case now. And PT-1707's diagonal keys cannot rescue a player boxed by four actual walls -- both flanks of every diagonal are wall, so no diagonal is legal, which PT-1613 already permits an author to build (a sealed room).

CAUGHT ITS OWN TEST TARGETING THE WRONG BOARD BEFORE SHIPPING: the original PT-1638 case walled all four orthogonals, which is not PT-1638's actual finding -- PT-1638's own sentence says "cannot leave WITHOUT STARTING A FIGHT," meaning a creature holds one side, not a wall. A held square is open terrain, so the corner beside it is not sealed. Rebuilt with a guard holding one side; the stranding hint now asks the same question the keys ask, so a refusal can never name a key that would do nothing.

ONE GUARD COULD NOT FAIL, ITSELF A FINDING: the dx==0||dy==0 early-return could not be broken by deletion, because with one axis zero the two terms being checked are squares every caller has already established open. Kept as the rule's documented scope rather than a gate, with the comment now saying so.

## PT-1713 -- DROID MELEE-CLOSURE: A VALIDATOR FAULT AT AUTHORING TIME, PLUS THE RUNTIME GATE. Not a silent hold in play

Coder found melee-closed-to-droids is wider than opportunity attacks -- three documents say it independently (ACTION-ECONOMY-01 4, CLASS-ATTACKS-01's four ranged-only chassis, SPECIES-CHAPTER-v2's Fixed Armature). Declined to build a silent runtime hold, correctly: enforcing the gate without a validator would mean a droid holding a melee weapon simply never acts, discovered by a player watching it stand inert turn after turn rather than by an author before the package ships.

RULED: Coder's own recommendation, taken as the ruling. A droid blueprint equipped with a melee weapon is a Loom validator fault -- an author learns at authoring time, the same family as PT-1379 (the Builder must not create a fault its own validator cannot detect) and PT-1646 (an unreachable area gets its own fault member rather than staying silent). The runtime gate ships alongside it as the second layer, so a droid that somehow reaches play still-equipped is refused rather than acting incorrectly, but the validator is the one that actually prevents the situation instead of merely catching it after the fact.

Sequencing per Coder's own preference, adopted: validator first. An author learns from a red fault in Loom before a player ever meets an inert droid in play.

## PT-1714 -- PT-1713 BUILT, BOTH LAYERS. A lightsaber closed for the right reason, kindFromSection moved to where it belongs, an async race caught before it shipped

PackageProblem.droidHoldsMelee fires for a placed creature AND one authored-and-never-placed, PT-1646's own case, "nothing else would have looked." The gate ships in both enemyTurn and the player's own strike -- the pair this corpus has found wrong fourteen times, applied to both paths in the same commit rather than one now and the other found later.

A LIGHTSABER IS CLOSED FOR THE RIGHT REASON, NOT AN ACCIDENTAL ONE: written as droidMayWield RANGED ONLY rather than NOT MELEE, because a lightsaber is its own kind under 12.5 and a naive melee check would have let a droid hold one -- FEATS-UNIVERSAL-01 closes it separately (Force-class only, droids cannot take the proficiency at all). Two rules landing on one answer, and the check reads that way rather than by accident. The mutation to != melee fails exactly the one case that distinction exists for.

kindFromSection MOVED OUT OF THE PLAY SCREEN because a second program needed the same answer -- which section is melee is a rules question, not a screen concern, and PT-1497's own sentence from a different field applies here verbatim: a reader in Loom would have added a third parser rather than reusing the one that exists.

THE CHECK NEEDS A SIBLING PACKAGE'S DATA AND SAYS SO OUT LOUD RATHER THAN SILENTLY DEGRADING: weaponSections comes from the caller because ENGINE-INTERFACE-01 4 bars the engine from reaching across packages itself, and an empty map disables the check with nothing on screen to say so -- stated at validatePackage, two tests holding both the positive (sections arrive) and negative (same package stays clean without them) cases.

AND A RACE CAUGHT BEFORE IT SHIPPED, NOT FOUND IN PLAY: the shelf read is async and verify fires on open, so a package opened before the read lands would validate without sections -- the droid fault silently absent for that one window. Fixed by re-verifying anything already open when the read completes.

A REAL GAP NAMED, NOT COVERED BY THIS RULING: nothing stops chargen handing a droid PLAYER a melee weapon. DROID-SKILLS-01 gates on skills, not equipment; the six starting kits are not chassis-aware. The runtime gate still catches it with a sentence, so it degrades rather than breaks -- but PT-1713's authoring-time half is only true for packages, not player characters. Coder's own read: the same rule half-applied rather than a new one, and recommended closing it before companions.

## PT-1716 -- PT-1715 CLOSED: THE SHIPPED DATA WAS ALREADY CLEAN. Three guards built anyway, one catching a defect worse than the one it prevents

Measured all three ways a droid could be handed a melee weapon before reporting anything: the nine droid arrays all name ranged weapons, none of the 21 profession grants is a weapon at all, and a droid on a class with no droid array gets no weapon rather than an organic fallback. Reported plainly rather than claiming a fix that wasn't there -- "a report that claimed a fix would be claiming a defect that was not there."

Built the chargen-side guard anyway, as the rule's missing half: equipmentPayload refuses to arm a droid with a non-ranged weapon and records why, reusing weapon_unresolved's existing vocabulary rather than inventing a new one -- "a save that cannot arm you should be able to say so years later." The refusal names the weapon it refused; a version that doesn't say which fails its own acceptance test. Lightsaber closed for the same reason as PT-1713's package layer, not because it's melee -- RANGED ONLY rather than NOT MELEE, so the distinction is structural rather than incidental.

A THIRD LAYER, NEARLY MISSED: a starting array is neither a blueprint nor a character, so neither existing guard covers it. If droid_arrays.toml ever named a melee weapon, the chargen guard would correctly disarm the droid -- and an entire class would ship with no weapon at all, a worse silence than the one being prevented. PT-1379's principle applied one level up, at the rules data itself rather than at play. A test over the real shelf fails with the offending array's own name in the message when this happens.

NOT DONE, NAMED CORRECTLY AS UNREACHABLE RATHER THAN SKIPPED: the equipment screen doesn't surface the refusal, because no shipped data can currently produce the case that would show it -- a sentence there today would be unreachable text, and belongs the day the data can actually trigger it.

COMPANIONS STARTING. Groundwork already in place and named before building: isParty (PT-1636, PT-1683) is already the one predicate the whole party question turns on; PT-1709's corner rule and §10's enemy-side trigger are both built and sitting idle, waiting only for a second party member to become reachable. Smallest honest first slice to be reported before building wide.
