## PT-1717 -- TO DO: A FACING INDICATOR ON THE BOARD. Queued for the art/visual design pass, not built

Owner: every token on the board -- player, companion, NPC, beast, enemy -- should eventually show which way it's facing, as some kind of arrow or directional mark. Explicitly deferred to whenever the visual design pass happens; this is a placeholder for the idea, not a spec.

⚠ CHECKED FIRST: no facing or orientation concept exists anywhere in the engine today. A placement carries a position (x, y) and nothing else directional -- there is no field a facing arrow could currently read. This is new state, not a rendering change on top of something that already exists.

There is a real precedent for WHY facing matters mechanically, not just visually, worth keeping in view when this is designed rather than treating it as pure decoration: STUDY 31 found KOTOR's own AI turns to face a target at half its detection reaction delay -- "it visibly notices before acting" -- meaning facing already carries information (who has noticed whom, before they've acted on it) in the system this project is closest to. Whether that becomes a mechanical fact here (a flanking bonus, a stealth check modified by whether you're in someone's facing arc) or stays purely cosmetic (an arrow that follows movement direction with no rule attached) is itself a design decision this ruling does NOT make -- it only files the idea and the one piece of prior art worth knowing about when it's picked back up.

Stylistic choices (the shape of the indicator, how it reads at token scale, whether it's a full arrow or a simpler notch) are explicitly the visual design pass's to make, per the owner -- not decided here.

## PT-1720 -- DROID PLAYER CHARACTERS GET DESIGNATIONS, NOT NAMES: CHASSIS PREFIX + TWO DIGITS, CHECKED AGAINST CANON. Owner ruling, queued

A droid player character does not choose a name the way an organic does. It gets a designation: the first characters come from its chassis (a T3 chassis droid starts "T3-"), followed by two digits, generated so the result does not collide with an actual canon droid's designation.

WORTH KNOWING BEFORE THIS IS BUILT: two canon-shaped droid designations already exist in this project's own fixtures -- T3-M4 (genuinely canon, Bastila's droid from K1, cited repeatedly across this project's own research) and T3-K9 (a Tester fixture name, not canon, but shaped exactly like one). Neither is a player-generated name under this rule -- both are hand-authored test/reference fixtures -- but T3-M4 is the live example of exactly the collision this rule exists to prevent, and worth using as the first canon name Coder checks the generator against once this is built.

NOT YET SPECIFIED, QUEUED FOR WHEN THIS IS BUILT RATHER THAN DECIDED HERE: where the canon droid-name list comes from (hand-maintained, or derived from something already extracted), what happens on a collision (reroll silently, or something visible), and whether a player can request a specific designation within the chassis-prefix constraint or the two digits are always randomly assigned.

## PT-1726 -- PER-MODEL DESIGNATION FORMATS, ALL SIX CHASSIS. Attested shape where the data has one, free choice where it does not

Pulled every model table in DROID-MODELS-01 directly rather than guessing. Two kinds of chassis fell out cleanly: those where a real designation example already exists to copy the shape of, and those where nothing in the source ever named an individual unit at all.

ASTROMECH -- ATTESTED, FOLLOW THE EXAMPLE. T3-series: prefix T3-, suffix two characters matching T3-M4's own shape (one letter, one digit). 3C-series: prefix 3C-, suffix two letters matching 3C-FD. T1-series: prefix T1- -- NOTE, T1-LB is flagged in the document itself as actually belonging to a separate LB-series rather than being a true T1 unit, so T1-LB is not a clean model for the format and the T1- suffix shape is inferred rather than copied from a same-series example. IT-series: prefix IT-, no individual example exists, suffix format inferred from the T3/3C pattern (two characters). R-8009 is its own line, not a T-step -- prefix R-, suffix matching R-8009's own four-digit shape. T2, per PT-1724, is the owner's own addition sitting in this line and takes T3's exact rule.

ASSASSIN -- ATTESTED, HK-SERIES. HK-24, HK-48, HK-49 are already the model lines themselves (product names, two digits) rather than individual-unit names layered on top of a model -- the same way T3-M4 layers a unit suffix onto the T3-series model, an HK unit's designation more naturally follows the format the games actually use: the two-digit number IS the individual identity for this series, so a player's HK-chassis droid is simply HK-[two digits not already a model name and not HK-47 or HK-50/51's exclusions]. HKB-3 is a distinct outlier shape (HKB- prefix, single digit) and stays its own case, not a template for anything else. The generic "Assassin Droid MK VI" model itself has no individual-unit convention attested -- free choice for a player who picks that model rather than the HK line specifically.

PROTOCOL -- MIXED, EACH MODEL HAS ITS OWN ATTESTED OR INFERRED SHAPE. 3DO-series: prefix 3DO-, suffix inferred (no individual example). GE3-series: prefix GE3-, suffix inferred. ET-74 is itself the only attested individual in that line, so ET- with a two-digit suffix, matching its own shape. GG-series: prefix GG-, suffix inferred. B-4D0 is flagged BACKTRACKED (PT-590) rather than a clean template -- its B-[digit][letter][digit] shape is noted but not treated as the definitive Protocol format given its own flagged status. The generic Protocol Droid model: free choice.

PROBE -- ATTESTED, THREE DIFFERENT SHAPES, EACH KEPT SEPARATE RATHER THAN AVERAGED. K-X12 (MerenData): prefix K-, suffix matching its own letter-digit-digit shape. CZ-P3 Miniprobe (Czerka): prefix CZ-P, single digit. SK-1 Seeker (Duwani): prefix SK-, single digit. Three manufacturers, three shapes -- a player's designation follows whichever model they actually picked, not a blended format. Generic Probe Droid: free choice.

BATTLE, LABOR, REMOTE -- NO ATTESTED INDIVIDUAL-UNIT CONVENTION EXISTS ANYWHERE IN THE SOURCE. Battle's models (War Droid Mark I-V, Assault Droid Mark I-II) and Labor's (Construction Droid Mark I/Foreman/Mark II, KM1 Mark I-II, Mover Droid) are all product-line names with Mark numbers, never an individual serial or call-sign in either game's data. Remote has no file entry at all (7's own flag). RULED, MADE UP AS THE OWNER ASKED, RATHER THAN LEFT BLANK: for these three chassis, a player has complete free-text choice of designation, subject only to PT-1722's canon-collision check and the general format rule that it must read as a droid designation rather than an organic name (no spaces, alphanumeric plus a hyphen, matching the visual convention every other chassis already uses even without a specific attested source to copy).

RULE OF LAST RESORT, STATED ONCE RATHER THAN REPEATED PER CHASSIS: wherever a suffix shape is INFERRED rather than copied from a real attested example, that inference is a guess dressed as a rule and should be revisited the day Researcher or Scholar finds an actual attested individual unit in that line -- flagged here rather than treated as equally solid to the attested cases.

## PT-1729 -- CORRECTION TO PT-1726: EVERY SUFFIX IS TWO DIGITS, NOT A COPY OF ONE EXAMPLE'S EXACT CHARACTER SHAPE

PT-1726 tried to match each chassis's suffix to the literal shape of its one attested example -- T3-M4's letter-plus-digit, 3C-FD's two letters, and so on. Wrong on two counts, both the owner's: the original instruction said two digits plainly, and a single example (one droid, one name) is not proof of a whole series' format rule -- T3-M4's "M4" could easily be a personal name riding on the T3- prefix rather than evidence of a technical letter+digit convention every T3 unit follows.

RULED, REPLACING PT-1726's suffix rule wherever it copied an example's exact character shape: every chassis and model with an attested prefix takes that prefix followed by TWO DIGITS, full stop. T3-, 3C-, IT-, T1-, R-, HK-, ET-, K-, CZ-P, SK-, GE3-, 3DO-, GG- -- each keeps its own prefix as PT-1726 established, but the suffix is uniformly two digits everywhere, not a per-chassis guess at letter-versus-number shape. Simpler, consistent, and gives the player a plain numeric field to fill or generate regardless of which chassis they picked -- exactly the "more freedom" the owner asked for.

R-8009's four-digit shape and HKB-3's single-digit shape stay as their own named exceptions (PT-1726 already treated both as outliers rather than templates), since those are the prefix-plus-number shapes actually attested rather than an inferred two-character guess.

Battle, Labor and Remote's free-text ruling from PT-1726 is unaffected -- this correction only touches the chassis that had a prefix-plus-suffix rule to correct.

## PT-1730 -- TEST 063: IDENTITY IS ALREADY PORTRAIT-FIRST, THE POPUP HALF IS WHAT DOESN'T EXIST. AND THE BLASTER-RIFLE BUG IS CLASS-INDEPENDENT, TWO SEPARATE DEFECTS

BASELINE FOR PT-1719, OBSERVED RATHER THAN RECALLED. Portrait-first is already true today -- no build needed for that half. What holds the name field is NOT a popup: Identity is three sequential full-screen routed steps (portrait, then a name text field with its own screen, then a story/bio preview), same chrome as every other chargen screen. So PT-1719's "name stays where Identity was, as a popup" is half-true of current code and half not -- the position is already right, the POPUP SHAPE is the actual work still to do. Useful correction to scope before Coder builds: this is narrower than rebuilding the step order, it's converting an existing routed screen into an overlay.

BLASTER-RIFLE BUG CONFIRMED CLASS-INDEPENDENT, NOT SOLDIER-SPECIFIC -- checked by reasoning about the right test rather than repeating the same string. class_arrays.toml gives each class a DIFFERENT stock weapon name (Soldier: Blaster Rifle, Scout: Blaster Carbine, Marksman: Marksman Rifle), so confirming scope meant testing the same FAILURE SHAPE on a different class, not the same literal weapon name. Built a second character on a different class with the same melee-upgrade choice: same shape, same wording, different weapon -- "equips items/weapons/blaster-carbine, which will not open: There is no item here."

TWO SEPARATE, NAMEABLE DEFECTS FOUND BY READING THE MECHANISM RATHER THAN GUESSING: (1) LedgerWriter.equipmentPayload computes weapon_r_1 purely from the class's stock array weapon via resolveStartingWeapon, regardless of any Equipment-step choice -- the melee-upgrade grant is recorded as item_unresolved ("nothing applies it yet") on every class it's offered to, and never actually replaces the stock weapon. (2) A package missing a class's stock weapon blueprint gets no warning earlier than a runtime "will not open" -- Loom's own verify did not flag this in either fixture package tested, meaning the gap is invisible at authoring time, only surfacing when a player actually starts a fight.

## PT-1740 -- CONDITIONAL DAMAGE VS A TARGET TYPE IS THE SAME SHAPE AS SNEAK ATTACK'S CONDITIONAL BONUS, NOT A NEW MECHANIC. Ion Blaster's "1d4 + 1d10 vs droid" gets a parser, not a ruling debate

TEST 065 found an Ion Blaster equips and silently swings as unarmed, because PT-1452's damage parser only reads a flat number or NdM, and equipment.toml's "1d4 + 1d10 vs droid" is neither -- refused correctly, fell back to a fist. Coder correctly identified this as squarely its own and asked whether the MEANING needed a ruling before building the parser, rather than assuming.

CHECKED FIRST: the corpus already has a precedent for exactly this shape. Sneak Attack and Stealthy Shot both add conditional bonus dice "against a target unaware of you" -- extra damage gated on a fact about the target, not a flat roll. Ion damage vs droid is the same shape with a different condition (target's kind, rather than the target's awareness state).

RULED: not a new mechanic, an extension of one already accepted. Parse "vs [kind]" as an additional damage roll applied only when the target's kind matches, same way Sneak Attack's condition already gates its bonus dice. This is also attested KOTOR behaviour rather than an invented rule -- ion weapons dealing bonus damage specifically to droids is real, established game mechanics, not something this project is choosing to add.

Coder's own sequencing stands: take it at the next pause, after companions' travel gap, since it's a parser extension rather than a blocker on anything currently in flight.

## PT-1744 -- STANDING RULE FOR AUTHOR: BORROW EXISTING PROSE AS MUCH AS POSSIBLE, MODIFY ONLY WHAT ACTUALLY NEEDS CHANGING

Owner ruling, permanent, applies to every future Armory chapter and every book after it, not just this one.

Where this project's own documents already carry human-written prose describing a rule -- explanatory text, worked examples, phrasing already crafted for a rulebook voice -- AUTHOR should reuse that prose directly rather than re-deriving the same content in its own words. Modify only what genuinely needs to change: a stale citation, a superseded number, a shift in scope between where the prose originally lived and where it's being placed now.

This is the same discipline already enforced on the engine side of this project, extended to writing: kindFromSection moved to a shared location the moment a second program needed it rather than being re-derived; roleNames became shared vocabulary rather than re-listed; PT-1436's whole rule against reinventing something that already exists. Prose is no different -- if EQUIPMENT-01 or ATTACKS-01 already states a rule in finished, rulebook-voice prose, that IS the chapter's material, not a source to paraphrase around.

Reason, stated plainly: the documents were often written carefully, by a human, specifically for this purpose -- reinventing the same explanation in different words is wasted effort at best and a drift risk at worst (two phrasings of one rule are two places for a future contradiction to grow, the same shape PT-1742 just found and fixed between ATTACKS-01 and EQUIPMENT-01).

Does not change AUTHOR's citation discipline -- borrowed prose still gets attributed to its source document precisely, the same as everything else AUTHOR has been checking and citing throughout this thread. And it does not license silently copying something that's wrong -- if the source prose itself needs correcting, that still routes the way PT-1742 routed ATTACKS-01's staleness, rather than being fixed in-line and left stale at its origin.

## PT-1755 -- BUILD 143: SECTION 10's ENEMY TRIGGER FINALLY FIRED, ELEVEN SLICES LATE, EXACTLY AS PREDICTED. AND A ZERO POOL FOOLED THE SAME CHECK A SECOND TIME, FROM A DIFFERENT CAUSE

BUILD 132 built the enemy-side opportunity-attack trigger and stated plainly it could not fire on any board that existed, because enemyTurn only ever closes on its one possible target and the party was one. PT-1735 made the party two. This slice drove it: a Sith adjacent to the player, its actual target a companion across the hall, reaching them means leaving the player's reach behind -- confirmed live, pinned by two mutations (severing the close-on call, and moving the snapshot to after rather than before the step).

⚠⚠ AND IT LOOKED BROKEN FOR THREE ATTEMPTS, FOR THE SAME REASON PT-1708 ALREADY NAMED ONCE. The test beds gave PlayScreen no characterClass, so the player's base attack bonus was null, the reaction pool computed to zero, and the trigger fired into an empty pool and returned silently -- geometry correct the whole time. Named as PT-1708's exact shape recurring on the opposite side of the same feature: a zero pool masking a working rule. The cause differed (a missing test-bed constructor argument, not an unwired engine seam), but the SYMPTOM was identical, and it fooled the same check twice.

⚠ THE DISCIPLINE WORTH KEEPING: Coder caught itself before filing this as a bug three boards in, by checking the cheapest explanation (a zero pool) before the more interesting one (broken wiring). PLAY-STATE-01 now records this as a standing heuristic -- a Section 10 trigger that appears not to fire is a POOL question before it is a GEOMETRY question. Worth remembering generally: when the same symptom recurs on a feature that already had one zero-pool defect, check the pool again before re-diagnosing the geometry.

A WOUNDED COMPANION WAS BEING QUIETLY HEALED BY WALKING THROUGH A DOOR, FOUND AND FIXED. _bringTheParty rebuilds a companion from its blueprint template on arrival -- full health, since a blueprint has no wounds. Fixed correctly, not by folding the transient blow itself: character.damaged is deliberately never logged (a blow is not in the log to fold, per PLAY-STATE-01's own stated lifetime rules), so what persists is encounter.ended, already written once per combatant. Coder wrote the fixture against the wrong event kind first and the projection's own doc comment is what corrected it -- a documentation comment doing its job.

THREE OPEN DECISIONS, RULED:

1. RECRUITMENT TRIGGER: a conversation effect, not a proximity walk-up or a new choice-on-meeting UI. Dialogue lines already support effect = [ { kind = ..., ... } ], with existing kinds like quest.flag-set and item.lost -- a party.joined (or equivalent) effect kind plugs into machinery that already exists, matches how the source games actually handle every companion recruitment (a conversation moment, not a proximity trigger), and needs no new UI built. An author writes the effect on the line where an NPC agrees to join.

2. SWITCHING CONTROL: parked, not decided. PLAY-STATE-01's own sketch of it depends on the unbuilt fog-of-war system (a droid and a Jedi genuinely seeing different things is what would make switching meaningful) -- deciding this now would be ruling ahead of the system it depends on. Revisit when fog-of-war exists, not before.

3. A FIGHT DOES NOT CROSS A DOOR: confirmed correct as-is, no change. Fight.abandon() and the transient round are the right shape -- the party crossing intact while the fight itself doesn't is the intended behaviour, not a gap.

Next: recruitment's conversation-effect kind, when Coder gets to it. The out-of-bounds silent _step return, PT-1640, and PT-1653 remain named and unbuilt, Coder's own call on sequencing.

## PT-1757 -- CHAPTER FIVE APPROVED, AND DecreaseAC RESOLVED DIRECTLY: A REAL PENALTY AGAINST A BASE VALUE NOT SHOWN IN THE SAME ROW, NOT A SEPARATE MECHANIC

AUTHOR correctly named a genuine gap in the property-list-alone reading rather than guessing: several Light-armour entries carry DecreaseAC with a negative value instead of the flat Armor N bonus most entries use, and the property list alone can't say whether that's below-category protection or a separate mechanic on an unlisted base.

RESOLVED DIRECTLY, TRACED THROUGH THREE FILES. Light Combat Suit (a_light_01, K2, 50 credits) carries DecreaseAC subtype 2, Penalty -1. Resolved subtype 2 against iprp_acmodtype.2da (confirmed identical in both games): row 2 is AC_Armor, not a narrower vs-melee/vs-ranged distinction -- this property targets the Armor component of AC specifically. The item's own BaseItem reference (38) points to baseitems.2da's own Armor_Class_4 row: baseac 4, dexbonus 5 -- a completely ordinary Light entry under chapter one's own sum-of-9 rule, confirming the base value AUTHOR correctly suspected lives elsewhere and isn't shown on the unique item's own row.

ANSWER: DecreaseAC IS a real penalty against that base, not a separate mechanic. Light Combat Suit's true net protection is +3 armor (4 base, -1 penalty), keeping the full +5 Dex cap from its category -- genuinely below-average for a Light item, consistent with its notably low price relative to other entries in the same category. Not a display quirk, not a second axis layered on top of an unlisted number that reads independently -- one number, reduced.

Chapter five approved on this basis. AUTHOR's five-representative-item scope for a 173-item catalogue stated plainly and accepted -- this is a browsable-reference chapter built on a primary-source catalogue that already exists in full, not a transcription task.

## PT-1762 -- ITEMS-08's HEADER MISMATCH IS NOT ARITHMETIC. TWO CONTRADICTORY SHOCK-ARM DESIGNS EXIST, BOTH CITING PT-713. OWNER DECISION NEEDED

AUTHOR flagged 42 (header) vs 69 (five categories summed) as an open gap, honestly stated rather than forced to reconcile. Checked directly: there are actually SIX category headers, not five -- "## shock-arm" appears TWICE in ITEMS-08.md (line 106 and line 181), and AUTHOR's sum only counted the first. Six categories sum to 73 (15+3+24+2+25+4), not 69 and not the header's 42.

⚠⚠ AND THE TWO shock-arm SECTIONS ARE NOT A DUPLICATE -- THEY ARE TWO GENUINELY DIFFERENT, MUTUALLY INCOMPATIBLE DESIGNS, BOTH CITING PT-713 AS THEIR AUTHORITY.

FIRST DESIGN (line 106, "THIS IS THE GENERIC LINE"): a purchasable item. Shock Arm costs 120 credits, Advanced Shock Arm costs 500, both use upgrade slots (melee/grip, melee/cell), gated by the Droid Upgrade feat chain for the second tier. Two tiers only.

SECOND DESIGN (line 181, "A GENERIC Astromech ARM, NOT T3-M4's"): no cost at all (every row shows a dash), no upgrade slots, no purchase or installation or bay of any kind -- instead it auto-upgrades on a fixed 1/7/13 character-level schedule, matching the ladder DROIDS-UPGRADE-01 already uses for Droid Upgrade and Plating Proficiency. Four tiers (I through IV), the fourth apparently replacing at level 19 though the prose only states "1/7/13."

These cannot both be true simultaneously. A rulebook cannot ship a droid's starting weapon as both a purchasable item with upgrade slots AND a free automatic level-gated chain with no purchase path at all -- a reader hitting either section alone would draft a completely different mechanic than a reader hitting the other.

NOT RULED HERE -- this is a real design decision, not an extraction fact. RULED options, for the owner to choose: (a) the purchasable/upgrade-slot version stands, the auto-upgrading version is deleted; (b) the auto-upgrading level-gated version stands, the purchasable version is deleted; (c) both exist as genuinely different things -- a droid's INTEGRATED shock arm auto-upgrades by level as chassis hardware, while a SEPARATE purchasable shock-arm ATTACHMENT exists as actual equipment, in which case they need different names and the contradiction is resolved by them not being the same item at all.

Neither AUTHOR's chapter nor this ruling picks one -- flagged plainly, same discipline as everything else this thread has caught.

The resref-name heuristic that worked for the Vibrosword family fails here on its own terms: K2 numbered these generically (w_melee_03, w_melee_08) rather than continuing K1's stunbaton-prefixed convention, which is exactly why matching by name alone missed the connection AUTHOR was right to question.

WHY THE DICE LOOKED WRONG: Stun_Baton's own base item die is 1d1 -- essentially no inherent weapon damage, consistent with an item whose real function is the Stun effect rather than raw impact. Same override mechanism already resolved twice today for droid plating's DecreaseAC and Bacca's Ceremonial Blade's DamageRacialGroup -- a base item type can carry near-zero inherent stats while individual items built on it carry their real numbers as properties.

RULED: these are Stun Baton variants, not undocumented base types. No addendum needed to Chapter One's established types. AUTHOR's family-sort can proceed treating both as part of the Stun Baton family alongside K1's own entry, sorted by their actual BaseItem reference rather than by resref name pattern -- worth AUTHOR checking BaseItem directly for any other K2 weapon whose dice don't obviously match a named family, since this is now the second time a name-based match has missed a real connection this session (Vibrosword's own five missed members, PT-1773, being the first).

## PT-1782 -- MARKSMAN RIFLE AND SNIPER RIFLE BOTH EXTEND THEIR WIELDER'S PERCEPTION RANGE TO MATCH THEIR OWN WEAPON RANGE, PASSIVELY, RESPECTING LINE OF SIGHT. Owner ruling, closes the mechanic; Sniper Rifle's own stats remain open

Owner wanted long-range weapons to be actually usable at their stated range, rather than theoretically reaching further than a wielder can perceive. Two readings were live: literal expanded board visibility (revealing tiles, fog-of-war), or extending the wielder's PERCEPTION RANGE specifically, reusing PT-1686's existing detection machinery. RULED: the latter -- fog-of-war does not exist as a system at all yet and would be a large undertaking unrelated to these two weapons; perception-extension delivers the actual gameplay effect asked for (a sniper can detect and engage what other weapons can't reach) using what is already built.

RULED PASSIVE, NOT ATTACK-GATED, FOR A MECHANICAL REASON RATHER THAN SIMPLICITY ALONE: an active-only version cannot work, because a target must already be perceived before it can be chosen as an attack's target -- extending perception only during the attack itself is backwards, the perception would need to already exist for the attack to be declared against something. Passive is the only version where the weapon does what it is for. Also matches how every other weapon property in this system already works (Balanced, Keen, and the rest are standing facts about the weapon, not activated abilities).

RULED, STATED EXPLICITLY SO IT IS NOT BUILT AS X-RAY VISION: extended perception still respects line of sight. A sniper rifle lets its wielder see FARTHER, not THROUGH things -- the existing canSee/line-of-sight checks apply on top of the extended range, not bypassed by it.

MECHANIC RULED, NOT YET BUILDABLE END TO END: Sniper Rifle is confirmed a brand-new, separate weapon from Marksman Rifle (owner confirmed directly), meaning it needs its own damage die, cost, range and threat range established before it can be added as a real base type -- the same shape as Training Lightsaber, Boots, and Shock Arm before it. ## PT-1790 -- BUILD 152: check_extracts REACHED STALE ZERO FOR THE FIRST TIME IN THE PROJECT. THE LAST STANDING FLAG WAS A REAL CODE LAG, CLOSED PROPERLY RATHER THAN SILENCED

STATE.md had recorded that re-stamping event_kinds.json would hide a real lag rather than fix it. Verified before touching anything rather than assumed: the rows re-extract byte-identical, only source line numbers move -- confirming the data was never the actual problem, the flag had been repurposed as a to-do marker. Closed the underlying code gap first, re-stamped second, clearing the flag for the reason it should clear rather than to make a red check go quiet -- the exact discipline PT-1608 already named (a permanently red check is one people learn to scroll past).

THE LAG WAS PT-1435's OWN DIAGNOSIS: a permanent event kind that no projection folds is the actual bug, while the check asking about it (emitted_kinds_test's handledByReplay) still assumed replay was the only projection -- true when it was written, false now that there are five. party.joined is folded by partyIn and by nothing in replay; asking replay specifically gave the wrong answer with no signal the question itself was wrong.

⚠⚠ FIXED WITH A SELF-MAINTAINING DESIGN RATHER THAN A SIXTH HAND-KEPT LIST: each projection now declares what it folds beside its own definition, and the full set is a computed union across all five rather than something a person has to remember to update when a projection is added. Deliberately final, not const -- two projections folding the same kind is normal and expected (character.died by two, encounter.ended by two others), and a const Set would have silently rejected the duplication a correct union needs to allow.

⚠⚠ NAMED A SUBTLE TESTING TRAP BEFORE FALLING INTO IT: a union of five stale declarations reads as more thorough than one stale list while being exactly as wrong. Built a case that reads each projection's actual source code, excludes the declaration line itself so the claim can't validate itself, and checks both directions -- a projection declaring less than it actually folds, and declaring more. Mutated both ways.

RIFLES SHIPPED AND VERIFIED: Sniper Rifle (1d12/50m/19-20/energy) and Marksman Rifle (1d10, item entry matching, two-handed and movement restrictions removed) -- each change checked against the actual diff rather than assumed correct. A new case asserts all three rifles share energy damage and 19-20 threat together, PT-1786's ruled shape made into a real guard.

THE CHECK INFRASTRUCTURE VALIDATED ITSELF AGAIN, UNPROMPTED: PT-1788's Sniper Rifle catalogue row landed one commit after its base type mid-push, and check_extracts flagged it on the pull, check_shelf named the specific stale file before it was ever copied -- three slices after being built, catching a real gap nobody had to remember to check for by hand.

⚠⚠ HONEST FLAG, NAMED RATHER THAN QUIETLY LEFT: PT-1782's perception-extension property reaches no shipped field. EQUIPMENT-01's ranged table has five columns and the property lives in prose beneath it -- equipment.toml ships both rifles without it, and nothing in the app currently extends perception from a weapon or lets canSee take one as input. Ruled-and-unbuilt, not shipped-wrong -- correctly not built this slice, since the actual ask was re-extract and re-ship, not new mechanics. Named explicitly as the same shape that let PT-1718 sit unbuilt for months: prose a table cannot carry is exactly the kind of gap that survives by being invisible to every check built so far.

## PT-1817 -- BUILD 156: PT-1137 BUILT, GRID TOKENS ARE NOW THE SIDEBAR'S OWN PORTRAIT. A WRONG EQUALITY ASSUMPTION CAUGHT AND RE-DERIVED INTO THE TWO PROPERTIES THAT ACTUALLY MATTER

Role read from the live log rather than the raw placement, for a sharper reason than the usual PT-1551 style argument: PT-1745 lets a conversation recruit a companion mid-game, so a placement's own role field records who someone STARTED as while the log records who they ARE now. Equality was never the real relationship. What was re-derived instead: containment (the board may know about more than the sidebar shows) and disjointness (the sidebar must never call a friend an enemy) -- both now asserted, with disjointness correctly identified as the one that would actually catch a real defect, since misclassifying an ally as hostile is the failure that matters to a player. The two drawings now share one source (isParty over _here) rather than remaining two independently maintained lists -- two lists that can disagree eventually do.

## PT-1823 -- BUILD 157: THE CLASSNAME "CASING BUG" WAS TWO DIFFERENT KINDS OF VALUE, NOT A CASING ISSUE -- CAUGHT BEFORE THE NAIVE FIX SHIPPED SOMETHING WORSE. §3a's EXPLORATION CATALOGUE BUILT AS AN ENGINE CONSTANT WITH THREE VERBS DELIBERATELY LEFT UNREACHABLE AND ASSERTED AS SUCH

Test's reported className inconsistency was correctly re-diagnosed rather than patched as reported. The player's row and a companion's row were never reading the same KIND of value -- ClassRecord.name (a real display name) against character.characterClass (the raw blueprint class id). They coincide for single-word classes only by accident, which is exactly why it read as a casing difference; bounty_hunter cannot become "Bounty Hunter" under any capitalisation scheme. The real fix resolves the id through the same classes map baseAttackAt already reads, with the raw id kept as a deliberate fallback for a blueprint naming a class the rules don't carry -- so a real typo stays visible rather than getting silently smoothed into a confident-looking wrong label. Also caught, same slice: the test bed covering this had never been passed the classes map at all, meaning it could not have caught this failure even in principle -- PT-1708's shape recurring in a different test bed, the product itself was fine (main.dart always filled it correctly), only the test was blind. Fixed.

§3a's exploration catalogue built as a table plus a filter, correctly not treated as a sixth combat budget -- combat's closed catalogue exists specifically because fairness requires identical defined choices under pressure, and exploration carries no such pressure. The catalogue itself lives as an engine constant rather than shipped data, matching the existing precedent of roleNames, gateKeys and engineWrittenKinds -- a closed vocabulary the product owns belongs in the engine, not something a package should be able to invent. Every skill a verb references is still checked against the actual shelf, so a verb naming a skill that doesn't exist would be caught rather than silently rolling nothing.

⚠⚠ THREE VERBS (SEARCH, TRACK, EXAMINE) LEFT DELIBERATELY UNREACHABLE, ASSERTED RATHER THAN HIDDEN. PT-1122's three party-directed verbs built on PT-1804's sidebar. Correctly REPAIRED rather than regenerated, for a reason worth keeping visible: blind regeneration would have silently overwritten every hand-ruled correction made across this entire session in the same files -- the x3 reverts, the threat-range fixes, the authored Marksman and Sniper rows. A search by the RETIRED TERM itself, rather than by document name, is what caught this, and is the method that would catch the next one.

## PT-1837 -- SIDEBAR PRESENCE SHOULD BE PARTY MEMBERSHIP, NOT PHYSICAL CO-LOCATION. Owner ruling, modeled on Baldur's Gate 3

A companion's presence on the sidebar should be tied to whether they are in the player's roster at all, not whether they are physically standing in the currently-loaded room or area. In single-player, every companion the player actually has counts as "with them" and should show on the sidebar continuously -- the same model Baldur's Gate 3 uses for its own party, where the whole roster stays present and controllable regardless of area transitions. The only thing that should actually remove a companion from the sidebar is the player specifically leaving them behind before entering combat.

NOT YET CONFIRMED WHICH MODEL THE CURRENT BUILD ACTUALLY USES -- routed to Coder to check directly rather than assumed. If sidebar membership is already sourced from party roster status (isParty) rather than physical co-location (_here), this may already be correct behavior; if it is gated by area co-location, it needs fixing to match this ruling.

## PT-1840 -- BUILD 160: PT-1838 CONFIRMED EXACTLY RIGHT -- THE SIDEBAR WAS ROOM-GATED, NOT ROSTER-SOURCED. FIXED WITH REAL DESIGN WORK RATHER THAN A NAIVE ONE-LINER, AND A THIRD SIGHTING OF SIDEBAR-AS-BOARD-PROXY CAUGHT IN ITS OWN PRIOR TEST

Confirmed precisely: PartySidebar itself carries no location filter at all, rendering whatever it's handed. The actual gate lived one line up, in play_screen's own _sidebar getter -- isParty was applied AS A FILTER INSIDE _here (the current area's placements) rather than being the membership source itself. Since _here resets on every area entry, this made the sidebar effectively room-gated despite isParty's own logic being roster-based underneath it.

⚠⚠ A GENUINELY SHARP DIAGNOSTIC INSIGHT: the room-based and roster-based readings could not actually disagree until Solo Mode existed, because _bringTheParty always brought every member the room hadn't already declared, so _here always contained the whole party in every previously reachable scenario -- PT-1468's exact shape, two answers to one question staying invisible while they happen to agree. Wait Here (PT-1122) was the first feature to create a real scenario where they diverge -- a companion holding position in a different room was still genuinely in the party and simultaneously invisible to the one surface that could offer them Follow/regroup.

THE FIX REQUIRED REAL DESIGN WORK, CORRECTLY NOT A NAIVE ONE-LINE SOURCE SWAP: sourcing from partyIn alone would have produced three separate wrong readings for an absent member -- the wrong tag name (re-opening PT-1795's already-fixed defect from a different angle), a nonsensical "0 of 10," and present:false incorrectly printing fight-specific language outside combat. Correctly resolved through combatantsIn with _restore applied instead, so a wounded companion doesn't display as full health. Explicitly NOT placed on the board -- nothing added to _here, so no range check or walk-into interaction can reach them -- with their real position drawn from PT-1122's own WaitingOrder record, confirmed by reading combatantsIn's actual function body rather than assumed. A new elsewhere field added rather than reusing present or holding, specifically to avoid baking in today's coincidence that the only way to be elsewhere is to be holding position -- good, forward-looking naming discipline.

⚠⚠ A GENUINELY HUMBLING, WELL-HANDLED SELF-CATCH: BUILD 158's own solo-mode test had asserted a companion should be ABSENT from the sidebar in a different room, reasoning "nothing put them on this board" -- true about the board, but the assertion was reading the sidebar, meaning this exact test had been actively pinning the bug in place as correct, expected behavior. Named explicitly as the THIRD instance of this file using the sidebar as a proxy for the board, with BUILD 159 already having caught two others -- and the pattern is now named directly inside the test itself, so a fourth instance gets caught by reading the test rather than by luck.

Switching control confirmed untouched, still correctly parked behind fog-of-war. Lodestar (the engine) untouched entirely -- correctly scoped as purely a question of which data source the screen reads from, minimal blast radius. Mutation-checked properly: reverting the source fix fails both the new case and BUILD 158's own solo-mode case that had been silently validating the bug.

No corrections needed. Approved in full.

## PT-1841 -- OBSERVED: ROOM STATE (POSITIONS) MAY NOT PERSIST ACROSS RE-ENTRY, AND COMPANION LANDING POSITION ON A SHARED DOOR CROSSING IS UNSPECIFIED. Owner observation from live testing, queued for next Coder work, not urgent

CHECKED AGAINST THE CORPUS FIRST. Two adjacent things are already deliberately ruled and NOT what this is about: fight/turn state correctly does not persist across a door crossing (PT-1755, confirmed as the right shape, not a bug), and wound/vitality state DOES already persist through an abandoned fight (a real earlier bug -- Fight.abandon() wrote nothing, losing the wound along with the round -- already found and fixed). Neither of those is what the owner observed.

THE OBSERVATION: during live testing, a fight moved enemies around a room, the player left through a door, and re-entering through a DIFFERENT door showed positions reset rather than reflecting where things actually ended up. Position memory for a room specifically -- as opposed to fight state or wound state -- is not confirmed addressed anywhere in the corpus either way. A real, distinct gap from what's already been settled, not a re-litigation of the door-crossing ruling.

OWNER PREFERENCE, STATED FOR THE RECORD: a room should remember its own prior state (positions of what's in it) when the player leaves and later returns, rather than resetting to a default spawn layout. And when a companion travels through a door WITH the player, they should land at a position that makes spatial sense relative to that door/entry point, rather than an arbitrary default. If a companion instead STAYS BEHIND in a room, that room needs to remember the companion's position too, consistent with the same room-memory principle.

NOT URGENT, QUEUED: owner explicitly framed this as something to keep in mind for the next round of Coder work rather than an immediate fix. Not yet scoped, not yet assigned -- captured here so it isn't lost, to be raised with Coder when that work resumes.

The last 22 orphan rows closed on genuine proof rather than a guess, matching PT-1832's own method requirement. Twenty-one more resolved by demonstrating the specific pairing is IMMATERIAL -- every row in each group carries identical text, every candidate carries an identical blueprint description, so any assignment produces a byte-identical document. Fixed directly in AUTHORED-CHARACTER-01's own schema example -- added a [skills] section mirroring the beast model's points-per-level shape, with individual skill ranks authored explicitly only where a specific scripted check will actually roll against that creature, left at zero otherwise. ## PT-1844 -- READER-FACING CITATION SWEEP: REMOVE ALL INTERNAL DEVELOPMENT-DOCUMENT REFERENCES FROM EVERY BOOK. STARTS NOW, ONE CHAPTER AT A TIME, NOT ONE GIANT PASS. Owner ruling

REAL PROBLEM, CONFIRMED BY SAMPLING RATHER THAN ASSUMED: both finished books cite internal MAIN_WORK development documents and ruling numbers throughout -- CANON-01-v2, PT-numbers, METHOD-RECORD-01, D-W-prefixed decisions, and more -- as though a reader could look them up. They cannot; these were never reader-facing, they are the coordination record between MAIN, AUTHOR and Coder. A five-chapter sample (Timeline 1, 2, 5; Armory 1, 7) found between 8 and 25 internal citations per chapter. Across 24 total chapters this is a large, systemic problem, not a one-off passage.

PRIORITIES, IN THE OWNER'S OWN ORDER: accuracy first -- the underlying facts must remain exactly as correct as before, nothing loosened or softened in the process of removing a citation. Streamlining and accessibility next -- a reader should never need outside knowledge of this project's own development process to follow a sentence. Clarity throughout.

METHOD FOR EACH CITATION FOUND: first ask whether the sentence needs any citation at all for a reader -- most do not, since a history or reference book does not normally cite its own internal editorial process, only its real sources. Where a citation is genuinely useful to a reader, point to something they could actually access -- a real published book, the games themselves -- not the internal ruling that established it. Where no external source exists behind an internal ruling, state the fact plainly with no citation rather than inventing one. The bibliography's own already-approved verified/unverified marking is the model to extend into body text, not a new standard.

SEQUENCING: STARTS NOW. One chapter at a time, each its own dedicated pass separate from other editorial work, submitted and reviewed individually rather than batched -- many smaller passes rather than one large sweep, per the owner's explicit instruction. Galactic Timeline first (eight chapters, the book where this was found), then the Armory (sixteen chapters). PHB work stays on hold throughout, unaffected by this.

## PT-1860 -- BUILD 164: THE REFUSED-SWING REVEAL BUG FIXED PROPERLY, TRANSIENT HIDING EXTENDED TO DOORS, A PRE-EXISTING PANEL OVERFLOW FOUND AND CORRECTLY DEFERRED. RULED: CASTING ANY POWER REVEALS, REGARDLESS OF TARGET

The refused-swing bug fixed at its real root: the original BUILD 162 placement only actually protected one of four refusal paths, not all of them as claimed -- already-acted, a droid with nothing to swing, and out-of-reach all still revealed a player for a swing that never happened. Correctly acknowledged as Tester's own diagnosis being right that this is the common case, not an edge case, since hiding spends the Action and hide-then-attack in the same turn hits canAct's refusal every time. Fixed by moving the reveal beside spendAction() itself, so revealing only happens exactly when the Action is actually spent -- matching a principle already stated nearby. Regression test reproduces Tester's exact reported path.

Good proactive extension found while fixing the above, not separately reported: Hidden now correctly ends at a door crossing as well as at a save, on the same reasoning that already justified its transient lifetime -- opposed against one specific encounter's enemies, carrying it past that fight or into a new room would create a condition nothing could ever properly end.

⚠⚠ PRE-EXISTING PANEL OVERFLOW FOUND, CORRECTLY NOT FIXED INLINE, ROUTED FOR SEQUENCING RATHER THAN FORCED INTO A BUG-FIX SLICE. A real, measured overflow (7.4px at a specific scale and entry count) with the general shape of its fix already anticipated by an old ruling (a full fight shortens the list, not the board) -- but which specific part of the panel should yield under pressure is a real layout decision, correctly kept out of scope for what was meant to be a targeted bug fix. Acknowledged as real and queued, not assigned urgent priority absent any sign it's blocking something.

⚠⚠ A GENUINELY GOOD SELF-CAUGHT METHODOLOGY ERROR: the first attempt to isolate whether the new indicator caused the overflow (by removing it and re-testing) was itself invalid -- removing the indicator made the test fail EARLIER, at an assertion expecting to find it, so the test never actually reached the overflow measurement at all and reported a falsely clean zero. Correctly recognized as a check aimed at the wrong subject, and explicitly tied to an existing standing caution about suspiciously clean zero results -- a good instance of applying a lesson to one's own fresh diagnostic work, not just to code already shipped.

Indicator correctly repositioned to the name line -- the row's most prominent position, adding no height in a panel with none to spare, better satisfying PT-1108's visibility requirement than the prior dimmed dot-joined treatment.

RULED: CASTING ANY POWER REVEALS A HIDDEN CHARACTER, TARGETING AN ENEMY OR AN ALLY ALIKE. Coder correctly reasoned the enemy-targeted case to yes already (a power aimed at an enemy counts as a declared attack per its own rule) and correctly declined to invent an answer for the ally-targeted case rather than guess. Reasoning for extending yes to allies too: the actual mechanism that breaks cover for an attack is not hostility, it is the overt, observable act of doing something while trying to remain unseen -- the swing itself reveals regardless of whether it connects, and casting is the same shape of action regardless of who it targets. ## PT-1869 -- BUILD 165: CASTING REVEAL BUILT CORRECTLY. A REAL PRIOR FINDING WITHDRAWN WITH FULL HONESTY -- THE PANEL OVERFLOW WAS A TEST-BED ARTIFACT CODER ITSELF CAUSED, NOT A PRODUCT DEFECT. TWO MORE SELF-CAUGHT TEST WEAKNESSES. RULED: A FALLEN COMBATANT SHOULD NOT DISPLAY AS "HIDDEN"

PT-1845 (casting reveals regardless of target) built cleanly, correctly applying BUILD 164's own swing-reveal lesson from the start rather than repeating the mistake -- placed after every refusal and beside the spend, so an unpayable power, an excluded target, or no target at all are all correctly treated as acts never taken.

⚠⚠ A REAL PRIOR FINDING WITHDRAWN, WITH GENUINE HONESTY ABOUT ITS OWN ROOT CAUSE: BUILD 164's reported panel overflow was never a product defect. hide_test's MediaQuery told the app a 1280x720 viewport while flutter_test's actual default surface was 800x600 -- a mismatch between what the app was told and what it was actually rendered into, producing an overflow that exists only in the test bed. Traced to its real origin rather than left as "found, cause unclear": earlier this same session, a setUp call that correctly sized the test view was removed as deprecated, following an analyzer's correct suggestion about the API while missing what that call had actually been doing. "The analyzer was right about the API and I was wrong about the purpose" is exactly the right way to state that mistake. Handled with full transparency -- STATE.md corrected, and BUILD 164's original claim kept in place with the withdrawal appended rather than deleted, since a withdrawn finding that vanishes is one nobody could ever check. The queued layout item is confirmed to have nothing behind it and can be dropped.

⚠⚠ A RELATED SELF-CAUGHT TEST WEAKNESS, FOUND ONLY BY THE HABIT OF MUTATION-CHECKING AFTER WRITING: the first casting-reveal test was a guard that could not fail -- it would have passed even against a build with the reveal code entirely removed. Casting also adds a status line that grows the row, scrolling the relevant content out of the test's default viewport, so the finder reported "not found" regardless of whether the reveal actually worked. Fixed by asking with skipOffstage disabled and asserting the row's continued presence directly rather than trusting a finder that could silently miss its own target. Correctly named as the same class of mistake as BUILD 164's invalid diagnostic, one layer down -- the discipline of deliberately trying to break a test after writing it is confirmed, concretely, as the only reason this was caught rather than shipped green and worthless.

The fight-to-the-end test's return surfaced one more real, honestly-named finding rather than a silent fix: a fallen combatant is included in the same _concealed set that drives the "hidden" display, which is technically correct by the code's own construction (not drawn is not drawn, regardless of why) but reads oddly to anyone seeing a dead character's row still say "hidden."

RULED: SEPARATE THEM. A fallen combatant's row should not display as hidden, even though the underlying not-drawn mechanism can stay shared. "Hidden" implies an active, voluntary choice to conceal; a corpse isn't making one, and showing the same word for two semantically different reasons is confusing rather than merely imprecise. The display layer should distinguish fallen from actively-hidden even if the underlying set membership doesn't need to.

## PT-1887 -- BUILD 168: THE NAME-REVERSION BUG DIAGNOSED PRECISELY -- THE FALLEN LEAVE PLACEMENT WHILE THE FIGHT STILL LISTS THEM, A GENUINE WINDOW WHERE THE ROW EXISTS AND ITS PLACEMENT DOESN'T. THE PARTY CASE CONFIRMED GENUINELY DIFFERENT, NOT A DUPLICATE. TWO TESTS CORRECTLY REFUSED SHIPMENT FOR PASSING FOR THE WRONG REASON

Tester's own dismissed candidate cause turned out to be correct after all, just located at a call site nobody was checking: of four _stillHere call sites, the obvious one (_endFight) is not responsible. _theFallenLeaveTheBoard() removes a dead creature from placement immediately on falling, mid-fight (an existing rule), while the fight's own order deliberately keeps them listed so the sidebar can still show them (a separate existing rule) -- creating a real window between the killing blow and the fight's resolution where the row genuinely exists and its placement genuinely does not. A clean instance of two independently-correct rules producing an unanticipated interaction, not a simple oversight in either one. Correctly recognized as PT-1795's defect shape appearing in a state its original design never considered -- that fallback was built for a blueprint that won't open at all, not a placement that has simply left. Reproduced first in an existing test already driving the exact window (the "check for an existing bed first" commitment from a few builds back, now visibly paying off), fixed by remembering the name at the moment a placement arrives, since departure is exactly when the normal lookup path stops reaching it.

THE PARTY QUESTION CONFIRMED GENUINELY DIFFERENT, NOT A DUPLICATE, WITH REAL EVIDENCE: an enemy's state goes to dead at zero vitality, immediately triggering the placement-removal that causes the bug; a party member's state goes to DOWN at zero, not dead, per an already-established ruling that neither current damage mechanism kills a party member at exactly zero -- true death only past negative Constitution. The reported defect literally cannot arise for a companion at zero, confirmed by the actual state machine rather than assumed from surface similarity. Tester's instinct to treat this as a real, separate question rather than an assumed duplicate is vindicated directly.

⚠⚠ GENUINELY HONEST ENGINEERING ON THE TRULY-DEAD-COMPANION CASE: covered by the code's own construction in principle, but two different attempts to build a verifying test both passed for the wrong reason (one accidentally matched the PLAYER's own struck-down text rather than the companion's), both caught by mutation-checking, and correctly neither shipped. Refusing a green-but-meaningless test in favor of stating plainly that the case is unobserved, rather than claiming coverage that doesn't exist, is exactly the discipline this whole session has been built around.

RULED: BUILD THE FIXTURE. A player character with artificially high Constitution, able to survive an enemy strong enough to actually drive a companion past -Constitution without the fight ending first, is worth the real construction effort -- this is exactly the kind of narrow, genuinely-edge-case window where subtle defects have hidden all session. Approved to proceed.

acceptance_test's failure inside this slice's full run, passing alone, correctly identified as BUILD 167's already-diagnosed load flake rather than a new regression -- the standing practice working as intended.

## PT-1902 -- EFFECT MODEL PROPOSAL APPROVED IN FULL. RULED ON DURATION, VERIFIED AGAINST PT-24's OWN TEXT: THE /3 CONVERSION DOES NOT APPLY TO ITEMS. SHIELDS USE THEIR DAMAGE POOL AS THE REAL LIMIT

Checked PT-24 directly before ruling, not assumed from Coder's own framing: its own heading reads "Force power durations convert at printed seconds / 3" -- explicitly scoped to Force powers by its own title, not a general seconds-to-rounds rule that happens to have been demonstrated on powers first. This directly confirms Coder's own suspicion rather than merely permitting it.

THE OVERALL PROPOSAL APPROVED WITHOUT CHANGE. The sub-table shape over a compact string is correctly reasoned -- a compact string earns its place by mirroring an incumbent source cell, and there is no such cell here to mirror, so the more readable shape is the right one. All five fields are well-grounded against real existing conventions rather than invented loose: does's closed vocabulary drawn from the actual rows rather than guessed at, base/terms correctly reusing the engine's own existing Term type and PT-1326's derivation requirement, spends correctly kept per-item rather than derived from category given §3's own real, named exceptions. THE REFUSAL CHANNEL IS THE RIGHT PRIORITY TO CARE MOST ABOUT: modeling weaponFromBase's proven value/refusal/notModelled shape means an effect the extractor cannot parse produces a countable gap rather than either silent nothing or, worse, a silently wrong effect -- exactly the discipline that has kept every other extraction this session honest.

RULED ON DURATION:

(a) PT-24's conversion does not apply to items. It was scoped to Force powers by its own title and content; applying it to item durations would be extending a rule past what it actually decided, not reading it. Item durations need their own treatment, not a borrowed formula that happens to share units.

(b) FOR SHIELDS SPECIFICALLY: the damage pool is the real limit, and the printed duration is a ceiling that ordinary play is not expected to reach. The Energy Shield's own text already states this directly -- "200 seconds, or max damage taken" -- naming the damage pool as the actual constraint in its own words. Build shields against the damage pool as the effect's real limit; treat the printed duration as an outer ceiling rather than converting it to a literal round count.

FOR THE REMAINING NON-SELF-LIMITING ITEMS (adrenals and anything without a pool of their own): a direct /3 conversion clearly produces unusable results (a 66-round duration is absurd on its face), so this needs its own coarser treatment rather than either a literal port of the powers' formula or an unstructured guess. Send this back as its own focused follow-up once you have a concrete proposal for it -- the goal is results that read as "a meaningful chunk of one encounter" rather than an exact unit conversion, but the actual mapping is worth your own proposal given the same reasoning that made the rest of this proposal strong: grounded in the real data rather than invented from outside it.

GO AHEAD on everything else: the extractor, the shelf column, Gear's spendGear caller with the medpac as first consumer, and the refusal-channel discipline throughout. Duration for non-shield items is the only piece still open.

## PT-1920 -- RULED: THE TABLE DROPPED A ROW, NOT THE PROSE MAKING A LOOSE CLAIM. FIFTH THRESHOLD AT 36 CONFIRMED, CHECKED DIRECTLY AGAINST THE SOURCE TEXT AND THE MATH BEFORE RULING

Read SKILL-RESOLUTION-01 section 5.1 directly rather than trusting the transcription, and confirmed Coder's finding exactly: the table caps at four thresholds (4, 9, 16, 25, reduction floor of -4), while the prose one line below states an eight-part job costs 3 at level 30 -- requiring a fifth threshold, since 8 minus 4 is 4, not 3.

Verified the pattern convergence directly rather than taking "36 fits" on faith: the existing gaps between thresholds are 5, 7, 9 -- widening by 2 each time -- so the next gap is 11, landing exactly on 36. Independently, 36 is the next perfect square after 4, 9, 16, 25 (2 squared through 5 squared, next is 6 squared). Two independent derivations converging on the same number is strong evidence this is a dropped row rather than coincidence.

Checked one apparent objection before ruling rather than after: at a literal skill total of 30, only four thresholds are crossed (4, 9, 16, 25), giving a reduction of only -4, which would NOT match the prose's claim of cost 3 even with a fifth threshold added at 36. This looked like it might undermine the whole hypothesis. Resolved by checking whether "level" and "skill total" are the same thing in this document -- they are not, confirmed from the document's own earlier line: "a first-level specialist already saves one," meaning a skill total of at least 4 is reached AT LEVEL ONE, well above the character's own level number. Skill total is ranks plus ability modifier plus other bonuses, and grows faster than raw level throughout a campaign. A level-30 character reaching a skill total of 36 through normal skill investment, ability score, and feats is entirely ordinary, not a stretch -- the prose's "level 30" describes a character's level when they've also built up that skill total, not an assertion that skill total equals level.

RULED: reductionThresholds becomes [4, 9, 16, 25, 36], the dropped-row reading. Update the pinned test to reflect this as the settled answer rather than the disagreement it was correctly built to catch.

## PT-1924 -- DIVERGENCE 2 WITHDRAWN CORRECTLY, RULED PERMANENTLY IN FAVOUR OF THE CURRENT BEHAVIOUR: LATER, TESTED RULINGS SUPERSEDE THE EARLIER GENERAL DESIGN PRINCIPLE. DIVERGENCE 3 IS MAJOR -- NPC TARGETING BUILT ON THE WRONG DOCUMENT'S MODEL ENTIRELY, TARGETING-01 NEVER CITED

⚠⚠ THE WITHDRAWAL ITSELF IS EXCELLENT JUDGEMENT, WORTH NAMING DIRECTLY: reporting a divergence without first checking what depends on the current behaviour is exactly the incomplete picture this whole audit exists to avoid producing. Finding that three already-approved rulings (PT-1672's observable window between a killing blow and a fight ending, PT-1846's corpse-does-not-read-hidden fix, PT-1849's name-survives-death fix) can ONLY be verified through the exact row the proposed fix would delete, and correctly recognizing this as a genuine tie-break between an earlier general design principle and later, more specific, battle-tested rulings rather than a simple bug to just fix, is precisely right. Reverting rather than taking the tie-break unilaterally was the correct call.

RULED, PERMANENTLY: KEEP THE CURRENT BEHAVIOUR. A defeated enemy's row stays, labelled struck down, through the remainder of the fight -- matching how party rows already work. Reasoning: section 3's original concern was almost certainly the ambiguity of a corpse sitting at zero health looking like it might still be a live threat worth tracking -- and the current behaviour already resolves exactly that ambiguity through explicit, unambiguous labelling. The row is not silently sitting at zero health; it is clearly marked dead. Given the current behaviour satisfies the design principle's likely underlying intent while also being the only observable surface for three later, deliberately tested rulings, the later and more specific rulings correctly govern here. This is not the code diverging from a rule -- it is an early, general design principle being legitimately refined by later, more specific work built and tested against real behaviour. Divergence 2 closes permanently in this direction; no further action needed on it.

⚠⚠ DIVERGENCE 3 IS MAJOR AND CONFIRMED AS A REAL STRUCTURAL GAP, NOT A SMALL ONE. TARGETING-01 -- the document that actually governs which target an NPC attacks -- is cited zero times anywhere in the engine. What is built instead is an ordered preference-list model explicitly borrowed from SPACE-AI-01, the STARSHIP combat document, applied to a domain it was never written for. TARGETING-01 itself specifies something materially more sophisticated: a genuine scored model with banded distance, a closing bonus, attribution outweighing heat, a three-state last-exchange tracker, vitality as a tiebreak, and a separate heat mechanic for Force users -- none of which exists. Correctly and fairly noted that the foundational safety gates (reach, sight, not attacking the incapacitated) are substantially satisfied as simple filters even without the formal gate structure, one of them more strictly than the document requires -- this is not "nothing works," it is specifically the scoring and preference logic running on a borrowed model from an unrelated domain.

RULED ON DIRECTION: TARGETING-01 is confirmed as the actual governing document; the SPACE-AI-01-derived model needs to be replaced with TARGETING-01's own scored model, not merely supplemented. Given the real scale of this (a genuine rewrite of NPC targeting preference logic, not a small patch), this is ruled as real, high-priority future work, treated the same as click-to-move -- named clearly now, not rushed mid-audit, and not left as a third or fourth re-flagging later. Confirm scope once the audit's remaining batches are complete.

RULED ON SEQUENCING: Coder's own instinct is approved -- finish chargen's audit batch before starting the click-to-move build, since chargen is the oldest code and the most likely place to surface more instances of the same borrowed-model shape, and starting a large build before the picture is complete risks working against files the audit hasn't finished examining. The picker itself approved without reservation -- exactly matching the proposal already approved, correctly recognized as one question three verbs ask rather than three separate pickers, and every piece (Aimed vocabulary, ordinaryReachSquares reusing the same squaresBetween call the strike itself uses, the chooser generalized a third time from _castKey and _scanKey) genuinely reused rather than invented. ⚠⚠ CHECKED SKILL-RESOLUTION-01 DIRECTLY BEFORE RULING ON EITHER OPEN QUESTION, AND THE ANSWER CHANGES THE SHAPE OF BOTH. Section 6's own mode table lists Medicine under Effect mode exclusively, and Repair under BOTH Resource and Effect modes for different contexts. Section 5.3 confirms: Medicine's roll answers "how much did that heal," not whether it worked -- this is not a DC-gated pass/fail at all, it is a fundamentally different resolution shape where the roll itself scales the outcome. Repair's own Effect-mode text is narrowly scoped to "when a droid uses a repair kit on itself" -- a droid self-repairing, not a character repairing an ally droid via an Action. The picker's own Repair verb, consuming Repair parts on a target droid, matches Resource mode instead, which genuinely does need a DC.

RULED ON TREAT: NO DC. Treat resolves in Effect mode, matching Medicine's own explicit description -- a valid, reachable, wounded ally (already gated by the picker itself) is not refused by a further pass/fail check; the roll's own total directly determines how much healing is applied, the same "how much" framing the corpus already states outright. The specific formula converting a roll total into a healing amount is a further implementation detail worth its own concrete proposal, grounded in the same base-plus-terms shape the effect model already uses elsewhere, rather than dictated here -- but the MODE itself (roll scales magnitude, no binary gate) is now settled.

RULED ON REPAIR-VIA-PICKER: DC EASY (10), using the general task-difficulty ladder from section 2 -- Coder's original instinct to look there was correct, it simply applied to the wrong verb. This is Resource mode: a genuine pass/fail check that, on success, consumes parts per the already-ruled reduction curve and restores vitality using the chosen repair item's own already-modeled effect data, the same mechanism Gear already uses to apply an item's effect -- Repair-via-Action is the ally-targeting counterpart to Gear's self-targeting application, gated by a skill check rather than a fundamentally different mechanism.

The honestly-named coverage gap (no fixture yet exercises a successful pick-and-resolve path, only the refusal branches) is noted and correctly not glossed over -- worth building once the above rulings give it something real to resolve against, not urgent before then.

## PT-1930 -- A GENUINE, FOUNDATIONAL FORMAT GAP: NO PACKAGE CAN AUTHOR A CONSUMABLE AT ALL, EXPLAINING WHY THE EFFECTS COLUMN HAS BEEN READ BY NOTHING FROM THE START. TREAT AND REPAIR CORRECTLY BUILT TO BOTH RULINGS. DIRECTION RULED; CONCRETE PROPOSAL REQUESTED

Confirmed as real and correctly not worked around: checking before building rather than discovering mid-build, and verifying against the actual disk rather than inferring, is exactly right for a finding this foundational. EQUIPMENT-01's entire 38 base types are weapons and armour with weapon-shaped fields; item_open requires a legal base type to exist before a blueprint can be written at all; and even a hypothetically-written custom item would have no resref to reach the 625 effects already keyed to real KOTOR items. All six existing packages, fixtures included, confirmed to contain zero consumables on disk. The retroactive explanation is the valuable part: the effects column was never an oversight in wiring, because there was never a format that could produce anything to wire in the first place.

Correctly not proposing a fix, given this is a real PACKAGE-FORMAT-01 question rather than a bug -- the three shapes named (a new consumable base type, an optional resref field, moving effects onto base types) are a good, fair survey, and the argument against the third (fighting section 3's own naming of specific items like Medpac and Advanced Medpac as individually distinct rather than one shared category) is sound reasoning worth keeping.

RULED ON DIRECTION: THIS NEEDS BOTH A NEW CONSUMABLE BASE TYPE AND A WAY TO REUSE THE ALREADY-MODELLED, RESREF-KEYED EFFECTS -- not one or the other alone. A resref-only fix would let a package reference an existing KOTOR item's effect but never let an author create a genuinely new, custom consumable with its own authored effect -- which defeats part of what a package format is for. A base-type-only fix would let new consumables exist but strand the 625 effects already built against real KOTOR items, forcing them to be re-authored redundantly. Both together let a package either point at something that already exists or define something wholly new, following the same effect-model shape either way.

RULED ON PROCESS, consistent with how the effect model and the target picker were both handled: send a concrete proposal for the actual schema before anything is built against it. You have direct visibility into item_open's real constraints and the existing blueprint format's actual shape -- propose the new consumable base type's fields and how a blueprint would either carry a resref or author its own effect data directly, and it will get a real, specific ruling.

TREAT AND REPAIR BOTH APPROVED EXACTLY AS BUILT, NO CORRECTIONS. The additional reasoning about section 2's auto-succeeds column not applying here -- taking 10 is for unhurried skill use, and a combat Action spent inside someone's turn is inherently under pressure -- is correct and was not something I had explicitly specified; good, sound derivation from the existing text rather than an invented justification. Both modes correctly pinned in tests specifically because one word carrying two readings is exactly the shape that collapses under a later, well-meaning tidy-up. Repair's own success path correctly hitting the same consumable-authoring wall, and saying so on screen rather than silently succeeding into nothing, is exactly right -- consistent with every refusal-channel decision made this entire session.

## PT-1936 -- TEST: CLICK-TO-MOVE CONFIRMED ON ALL FOUR RULED CASES, BUT TWO REAL DEFECTS FOUND -- MOVEMENT DOUBLE-CHARGES PER SQUARE, AND AN UNREACHABLE TILE CAN REROUTE THROUGH A DOOR INTO ANOTHER AREA ENTIRELY. VITALITY BAND CONFIRMED CLEAN

Vitality band confirmed clean across three real samples including immediately after a hit landed and with two differently-wounded combatants -- band and sidebar agreed every time.

⚠⚠ DEFECT 1, SERIOUS: MOVEMENT DOUBLE-CHARGES PER SQUARE. approach() spends the live budget while it routes, and _step spends again replaying the same route -- every square costs twice. At speed 5, a 2-square click cost 4; a 6-square click spent the entire budget for no net movement. Precisely diagnosed as invisible until now because the exploration path used a throwaway budget rather than the real tracked one, so double-spending against it never had a visible consequence -- click-to-move is the first consumer to spend against something that actually matters.

⚠⚠ DEFECT 2, SERIOUS: AN UNREACHABLE TILE CAN SILENTLY REROUTE THE PLAYER THROUGH A DOOR INTO A DIFFERENT AREA. Clicking a floor tile behind a solid wall in the Probe Hall did not refuse -- the player crossed a door and arrived somewhere else entirely, reproduced twice. The wall itself was not walked through; the actual computed route came back non-empty with a door as its first leg, and the existing refusal only checks for an empty route rather than checking whether the route actually reaches the tile that was clicked. A player clicking a specific destination can be silently redirected somewhere they never chose.

Both routed to Coder as urgent fixes. Good discipline from Tester: correctly identified that difficult terrain could not be cleanly measured because the double-charge corrupts any budget-based observation, rather than reporting an unreliable result as if it were clean. Coder's uncommitted Treat/medpac work correctly left untouched and confirmed not to intersect either fix.

The self-caught dead-instrument mistake (a lookup using the wrong resolution chain, silently swallowing an exception for half the check, producing a uniform false negative across every row) is a valuable, generalizable diagnostic worth keeping: a check returning the identical result for every case tested is itself a reason for suspicion, not a clean finding, since real data rarely comes out that uniform on its own.

## PT-1944 -- ALL THREE RULINGS BUILT WELL. TWO SERIOUS MISTAKES SELF-CAUGHT BY EXISTING TESTS, THE SECOND WOULD HAVE BROKEN EVERY EXISTING NON-CREATURE PLACEMENT IN THE PROJECT. "ABSENCE IS NOT A CLAIM AND CANNOT CONTRADICT ONE" IS A GENUINELY VALUABLE STANDING PRINCIPLE

Tier-and-number approved exactly as built. Supplies count approved, with good, honest test-design correction: recognizing that a single-medpac fixture produces "none left" whether the underlying count logic is genuinely correct or just trivially always empty is exactly the vacuous-guard shape named repeatedly this session, and building a properly-scoped three-medpac bed instead is the right fix. ⚠⚠ BOTH SELF-CAUGHT MISTAKES ARE GENUINELY SERIOUS, AND THE SECOND DESERVES REAL RECOGNITION. The first (an overly narrow path check turning an already-known, already-reported fault into a hard failure) is a real regression correctly caught and fixed. The second is meaningfully worse and correctly named as such: treating an absent kind field as an active claim of creature, then refusing any blueprint that disagreed with that assumed default, would have broken every existing area that had ever placed a non-creature object by path inference alone -- which is the norm for all content that predates this feature. "Absence is not a claim and cannot contradict one" is worth keeping as its own standing principle beyond this one fix -- a genuinely valuable, generalizable piece of logic: the absence of a stated fact should never be treated as equivalent to an actively assertable value that could then conflict with something else. Worth applying anywhere else in the corpus where a missing field currently defaults to a value strict enough to be contradicted, not just here.

## PT-1968 -- OWNER RULING: NO-RETRY IS OVERTURNED. RETRY IS ALLOWED ON LOCKS AND TERMINALS, GATED BY REAL RESOURCE COST RATHER THAN A HARD REFUSAL. MINES GET A RICHER MODEL -- DISARM, RECOVER, SET -- WITH A FAILED RECOVERY RISKING DETONATION

Owner ruling, grounded directly in how the source games actually work: in KOTOR, a failed lock or slice attempt could be retried, including by spending spikes, and mines specifically support three distinct outcomes -- disarm (removes it, no reward), recover (disables it AND adds it to inventory as a usable item), and set (place a previously-recovered mine yourself) -- with a failed recovery attempt able to detonate the mine. The owner wants retry allowed, with failure meaning real resources get spent rather than the attempt simply being refused outright.

RULED: THE GENERAL NO-RETRY PRINCIPLE (PT-1501, and everywhere it has since been applied -- doors, and now due to extend to terminals) IS OVERTURNED. For locks and terminals, this connects directly and cleanly to a system that already exists: section 5.1's own resource-reduction curve already models exactly this shape -- spending a consumable (spikes for Security, presumably the equivalent for Slicing) per attempt, with skill reducing the cost. Retrying a failed lock or slice should be permitted as long as the resource to attempt it again is actually available; running out of spikes or parts is the real limit, not an artificial one-shot refusal. This is a genuine reversal, not a small adjustment -- update wherever no-retry was built (doors, and wherever terminals were about to receive the same treatment per the last ruling) to allow retry gated by resource availability instead.

RULED: MINES GET A RICHER MODEL THAN A SIMPLE DISARM-OR-NOT. Three distinct outcomes: disarm (the mine is gone, no reward), recover (the mine is disabled and added to the player's own inventory as a real, usable item), and set (a previously-recovered mine can be placed by the player). A failed recovery attempt specifically should carry real risk -- the mine can detonate, distinct from disarm's presumably safer failure mode. This is genuine new scope beyond what currently exists (a simple pass/fail disarm), not just removing a refusal -- treat it as its own real build, and send a concrete proposal for how disarm/recover/set map onto the existing hazard and effect systems before building it, matching how every other new mechanic this session has been handled.

Both pieces are real, substantial changes to already-shipped behaviour -- correctly scope them as such rather than small patches.
