## PT-2157 -- IMMUNE MEASURED, NOT BUILT, EXACTLY AS ASKED. RULED: IMMUNITY IS CATEGORICAL AND MUST WIN OVER ANY NUMERIC RESIST, EVALUATED BEFORE SUBTRACTION -- A REAL, ALREADY-EXISTING COLLISION, NOT A HYPOTHETICAL. DAMAGE IMMUNITY AND POISON+CRITICAL-HIT IMMUNITY PROCEED NEXT; MINDSPELLS/PARALYSIS STAY BEHIND THE CONDITION SYSTEM AS ALREADY RULED

**Approved in full, and the five-way split of what looked like one property is exactly the right instinct, now clearly a standing habit rather than something needing to be rediscovered each time.** Correctly recognising that poison and critical-hit immunity ride machinery that already runs, that mindspells and paralysis need machinery that doesn't exist at all, and that the two zero-reach categories fail for a DIFFERENT reason than the familiar blueprint shortfall -- creature-only items and an upgrade system this project has no model for, not a data-routing problem -- is precise diagnosis at real scale, not a template applied on autopilot.

⚠⚠ **A SECOND CORRECTION IN THE SAME REPORT, SMALLER THAN THE FIRST BUT THE SAME SHAPE, AND CAUGHT BEFORE IT BECAME THE ANSWER.** A four-day-stale string very nearly stood in as the answer to the exact question this whole slice turns on -- "does condition machinery exist." "A snapshot of what the build happened to contain was standing in for the rule" is a precise, generalisable way to name this: a comment or a string is a fact about a moment, and treating it as a fact about the design is the same error as the `g1_` prefix carrying a finding it never re-earned, just on a much shorter timescale. Good that the actual conclusion held up under the correct reasoning even though the reasoning that first produced it didn't.

### RULED -- DAMAGE IMMUNITY ORDERING

**Immunity is categorical, not a large number, and it must be evaluated before any resist subtraction runs, not folded into the same numeric merge.** A resist is a partial, quantitative mitigation; an immunity is an absolute, qualitative fact about whether a damage kind affects the wearer at all -- they are not two points on one scale, and representing immunity as a big resist number would be exactly the lie to the UI already correctly identified as unacceptable. The real, already-existing collisions -- three fire, one cold, one sonic, one electrical, all across-slot rather than within one item -- confirm this needs deciding now, not when it first breaks in play. Build it as its own check that short-circuits the resist merge when it fires, using the same reused pipeline for everything else, exactly as scoped.

### SEQUENCE

**Damage Immunity first** -- smallest, pipeline fully proven, only the ordering rule was open and it's settled above. **Poison and critical-hit immunity next**, 22 reachable items between them, both against live machinery, no dependency on anything still missing. **Mindspells and paralysis stay behind `PT-2152`'s condition-system ticket**, as already ruled and correctly not re-litigated here. Level/ability drain stays behind the ability-score hold and has no reachable item regardless -- lowest priority of everything on this board by a wide margin.

Good discipline building nothing beyond the two corrections and reporting the real shape first. Proceed.

## PT-2158 -- DAMAGE IMMUNITY LANDS. THE LIST-NOT-TABLE SHAPE MAKES THE ORIGINALLY-NAMED LIE STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE RATHER THAN MERELY DISCOURAGED. THE VOCABULARY FILTER IS THE WHOLE FUNCTION, AND ITS FAILURE MODE WOULD HAVE BEEN INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM SUCCESS. RULED: IMMUNITY SITS AHEAD OF `unstoppable` TOO, CONFIRMING A DECISION CODER CORRECTLY FLAGGED AS UNMEASURED RATHER THAN GUESSING SILENTLY

**Approved in full. Choosing a list over a table is the better implementation of `PT-2157`'s own principle, not just a compliant one.** A table with nowhere to stop a number would have needed discipline to avoid printing one; a list has nowhere to put one at all. Building the shape so the lie is structurally impossible rather than merely discouraged is the stronger version of the same ruling.

⚠⚠ **THE VOCABULARY-FILTER FINDING IS THE SHARPEST THING IN THIS REPORT, AND IT DESERVES TO BE STATED PLAINLY: THE BUG IT PREVENTS WOULD HAVE BEEN INVISIBLE.** A reader that stopped at `does == 'immune'` would have filed *immune to mindspells* as a damage kind literally named `mindspells`, which nothing real ever deals -- so nothing would ever have been immune to anything, and that state is indistinguishable from the state before this slice existed. A test that only checks "does the suite still pass" cannot catch a bug whose entire effect is that nothing changed. Pinning the exact four ids rather than a count is the only thing that could have caught it, and the report is honest about why: six is a real, wrong number this exact mistake would have produced.

**Confirming the correct call: immunity sits ahead of `unstoppable` as well, not only ahead of resist.** The reasoning holds -- `unstoppable` is a statement about the arithmetic below it (nothing reduces it), and letting it beat immunity would quietly re-admit the same category error `PT-2157` was written to close, just through a different door. Good, disciplined honesty labelling the fixture-based test as a decision rather than a measurement -- there is genuinely nothing in either game's real data that could settle this either way, and saying so in the test's own comment rather than letting it read as proven is exactly right. Confirmed as the ruling now, not left as an open, reversible guess -- this closes it rather than leaving it a standing question with a placeholder answer. Good instinct refusing `immune = ["unstoppable"]` at authoring time too; letting one item silently switch off the one guarantee this project makes about damage would be a much worse failure than anything this slice was built to prevent.

⚠⚠ **THE MUTATION SURVIVOR IS THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL FIND IN THE WHOLE IMMUNITY THREAD, AND IT LANDS ON THE SAME ITEM `PT-2156` JUST RESCUED.** Every test used belt- and mask-style items, so only one of `wornAt`'s two immunity-carrying exits was ever exercised -- and the untested exit is the one real armour takes, which means the one catalogue row carrying more than one immunity, `g1_a_class6001`, would have shipped with none of them actually working, silently, while every test stayed green. The same item nearly discounted as debris in the last report is the one item that would have been quietly broken in this one. That's not a coincidence worth shrugging past -- it's a reminder that the real, valuable content and the untested paths tend to be the same content, precisely because it's the content nobody had reason to look at closely before. Good, thorough closure with three real tests rather than one narrow patch, and good, honest correction of the one test that was itself wrong on the exact wording -- caught while writing the very fix meant to catch something else.

⚠⚠ **THE ROUND-BOUNDARY FIND WAS NOT ASKED FOR, AND IT'S THE KIND OF CATCH THAT JUSTIFIES LOOKING BEYOND THE LITERAL BRIEF.** An immunity that holds against a direct blow and silently fails against the identical damage type arriving as a tick is the same rule behaving two different ways depending on which code path it happens to run through -- exactly the kind of inconsistency a player would experience as "this doesn't work" without ever being able to say why. Confirming it's live rather than theoretical (14 poison-DoT sources, 19 poison-immune items, real overlap) rather than assuming it mattered, and noting it's the arithmetic poison immunity will immediately depend on next, shows this was fixed because it was found to be load-bearing, not fixed on principle alone.

### THE SCREENSHOTS -- HOLD, DON'T DECIDE BLIND

Correct instinct not committing binary diffs neither of us can account for. Don't drop them either without knowing why they changed -- discarding an unexplained change is exactly as blind as keeping one. Find out what touched them before either action; if nothing in this thread's own tooling explains it, that's worth knowing on its own.

Verification approved in full. Proceed to Poison and critical-hit immunity next, as sequenced.

## PT-2159 -- POISON AND CRITICAL-HIT IMMUNITY LAND. THE SCREENSHOTS RESOLVED PROPERLY -- ONE REAL, ONE PURE NOISE FROM AN UNSEEDED RANDOM, AND ONLY ACTUAL INVESTIGATION COULD HAVE TOLD THEM APART. AND THE STANDOUT: THE OBVIOUS IMPLEMENTATION WOULD HAVE TESTED CLEAN AND WAS STILL WRONG -- POISON IS NOT A DECLARED DAMAGE KIND, AND MATCHING ON A SHARED SPELLING IS NOT THE SAME AS MATCHING ON A SHARED MEANING

### THE SCREENSHOTS -- VINDICATING "DON'T DECIDE BLIND"

Approved in full, and worth stating plainly why this justified the wait: the two files needed opposite treatment, and no amount of guessing either direction would have found that out. `09-skills.png` was real -- `PT-2148` reaching the UI, correctly committed. `13a-identity-portrait.png` was never going to be anything but noise, built on an unseeded `Random()` whose output happened to be baked into the very image being diffed. "The harm was not the noise. It was that the instrument had stopped measuring" is the right way to describe what was actually broken -- not that one file was noisy, but that a noisy file sitting next to a real one meant neither could be trusted without doing exactly this work. Good, minimal fix: an optional seam nothing in the live app uses, verified by actually comparing bytes across two runs rather than assuming a fixed seed would behave.

### THE POISON DESIGN DECISION -- THE BEST FINDING IN THIS REPORT

⚠⚠ **THIS IS WORTH STATING AS PLAINLY AS POSSIBLE: THE EASY, OBVIOUS IMPLEMENTATION WOULD HAVE PASSED EVERY TEST AND BEEN WRONG.** Widening the damage-kind immune list to admit `poison` would have worked mechanically -- `Ongoing` carries a matching kind string, `afterResistance` would have matched it, every test would have gone green. It's wrong because `damage_kinds.toml` declares eleven real kinds and poison isn't one of them -- and "putting it in the damage set is a value used as a key" is a precise, exportable way to name the actual error: two facts sharing a spelling are not the same fact, and a system that matches on the spelling anyway is quietly asserting something the declared vocabulary says is false, even while producing the correct number today. This is the same root shape this whole session has named in different clothes -- inheriting behaviour from a resemblance rather than a real relationship -- caught here before it ever shipped rather than after. `g1_a_class6001` proving the split on one real item, immune to three genuine damage kinds and two things that explicitly aren't, is exactly the kind of concrete confirmation that turns an abstract principle into something undeniable.

**Declaring the honoured/unhonoured gap explicitly rather than silently dropping what can't be read yet is the right instinct, done well.** Twenty-one blueprints correctly carrying `mindspells` data nothing yet consumes, with a test pinning the exact difference between all five kinds and the two currently honoured, turns a future condition-system landing into a checklist instead of an archaeology project. Mutation confirming the silent-drop alternative actually dies is the right level of rigor for a decision this easy to get subtly wrong in either direction.

### THE TWO ORDERING ARGUMENTS -- BOTH GENUINELY EXCELLENT REASONING

**Checking immunity before rolling the save, for dice-sequence integrity rather than tidiness, is the sharper of the two.** A discarded roll still consumes a face from the fight's one shared dice source, silently shifting every subsequent roll -- and doing so only in the specific, easy-to-miss case where a poison-immune target happens to be poison-attacked, which is exactly the kind of intermittent, hard-to-reproduce corruption that could sit undetected for a long time. Tying this to `PT-1013`'s replay guarantee rather than treating it as a minor sequencing preference is the right frame -- this isn't about getting a slightly cleaner code path, it's about the fight's log remaining a true record of what happened.

**Gating the multiplier rather than the underlying threat roll is the correct distinction, and the reasoning for why is worth keeping as its own principle.** `toHit.critical` staying true to what the dice actually did, with only the downstream damage consequence suppressed, means the combat log never has to explain away a natural 20 that mysteriously didn't count -- the roll is honest, only its effect is blocked. Adding `DamageOutcome.critStopped` so the log says what happened rather than leaving a `× 1` that looks identical to a normal hit is exactly the player-facing clarity `PT-1326` already established matters -- a player should never have to guess whether their apparent crit "just didn't work" because of a bug or because of a real, in-fiction reason.

**The screen-level test choosing the log line over the vitality pool as its observable is a genuinely sharp piece of test design.** Recognising that identical death in both the immune and non-immune runs makes the pool useless as a discriminator, and finding the one observable that actually differs -- the specific sentence at the specific moment -- rather than accepting a green test that proves nothing, is real skill. The three-way check (control, immune, kindless-control) confirming immunity to one kind correctly does NOT suppress a crit from a different kind is the right extra mile.

Mutation approved in full -- fifteen run, all killed, no crashes. Good, small generalisation catching `_joined`'s two-argument ceiling before a fourth caller could silently stop being reported, and good, honest correction of two of your own test assertions against the real data rather than an assumed shape.

Nice, organic confirmation that `PT-2158`'s routing landed correctly -- Tester's own `immunity-probe` package, named fixtures matching the exact items just routed, found and correctly left untouched.

Verification approved in full. Proceed as sequenced: `skill` next, `save` after.

## PT-2160 -- TEST 092: RESIST, DEFENCE OVERRIDE, AND DAMAGE IMMUNITY ALL CONFIRMED CORRECT ON THE DIRECT-HIT PATH WITH EXACT ARITHMETIC. ONE REAL DEFECT FOUND: THE SPRING TICK AND THE BOUNDARY TICK DISAGREE -- `_springsAs` CHECKS NEITHER RESIST NOR IMMUNITY, AND THE FIRST TICK IS THE ONE NO PLAYER CAN EVER AVOID. RULED: FIX BEFORE PROCEEDING TO `skill`

**The methodology deserves approval on its own before the findings do.** Deliberately not running Edit Copy while Loom was mid-edit on the exact files it would have exercised, and hand-transcribing each test blueprint into the shipped writer's real format instead, is the correct way to keep "does the app read a blueprint correctly" cleanly separated from "does Edit Copy write one correctly" -- measuring unshipped work and calling it the palette would have been a real methodological error, and it was caught and avoided rather than walked into. Choosing a single weapon that deals two damage kinds in one blow so resist and immunity could both be exercised in the same swing is efficient, well-considered test design. The PT-number note is fine as flagged -- a routing note, not a defect, and the more precise citations are the ones worth keeping going forward.

**All three direct-hit confirmations approved as reported.** `t-desh`'s three-point gap between base and item value ruling out any possible misreading, `t-bastion` confirming silence correctly falls back to the base type, and the single item demonstrating both Defence override and resist in one blow are exactly the kind of decisive, unambiguous evidence this project has asked for throughout. Confirming the belt's "no defence column, immunity still carried" case specifically closes the loop on the exact untested exit `PT-2158`'s mutation testing flagged as a risk -- good that it was checked in real play, not just assumed fixed because the unit test now passes.

### RULED -- FIX THE SPRING/BOUNDARY DISAGREEMENT BEFORE `skill`

**This is a real, live, currently-guaranteed defect, not an edge case.** `endRound` correctly consults `resists:` and `immune:`; `_springsAs` consults neither, honouring only the save. Because the first tick is structurally unavoidable -- no player can reach the boundary ticks without taking the spring first -- this means every hazard encounter currently deals at least one tick of damage to a target the rules say should take none. That is a worse failure than an inconsistency that only shows up occasionally; it shows up every single time.

**The control confirms this is real, not an artifact of the test.** The no-resistance row continuing to take damage at every boundary tick, run to a full party defeat, rules out the boring explanation that the tick mechanism itself is simply dead -- a dead instrument would have produced identical-looking zeros. And confirming the same already-loaded immunity that failed at the spring correctly worked five times running at the boundary, in the same fight, rules out a loading race as the cause. Both real possibilities checked and closed before reporting the finding as structural.

**Correctly recognised as the same shape recurring, not a new problem.** `PT-2035` slice (c) already reconciled these same two paths for the damage EXPRESSION; this is the identical architecture disagreeing on a different aspect -- what's done to the amount, not the amount itself. Worth having both instances on record together: a dual-path structure that has already needed reconciling once is exactly the kind of place a second, different inconsistency tends to hide, and it did.

**Fix this now, ahead of `skill`.** The pointer that `_fight` is already in hand two lines below in `_springsAs`, with `resistsFor`/`immuneFor` already reachable through it, suggests this is genuinely small relative to its severity -- apply the same check `endRound` already runs, at the spring. Re-verify against the same live scenario used to find it (fire-immune target, poison-resistant target, no-resistance control) before calling it closed, not only against a new unit test.

### THE SECOND FINDING -- QUEUED, NOT URGENT

**Two catalogue rows sharing a display name with genuinely different mechanics (full immunity in K1, `resist 15` in K2) is correctly not a data-model defect** -- `PT-2059` already made the id the real identity for exactly this reason. It is a real palette clarity gap: nothing in the Loom browsing view currently distinguishes the two under one shared name, and the difference is categorical, not cosmetic. Correctly, honestly noted as currently invisible in play, since nothing in the corpus deals more than 15 fire or electrical damage in one hit today -- low priority, but worth a line on the standing queue so it doesn't quietly become a real problem the day a stronger attack is added: the palette should show enough to tell a true immunity apart from a large resist under one name.

Everything explicitly not tested (cold/sonic, Droid Quadranium Armor, the 81 effect-vocabulary immunities, Edit Copy itself) is correctly out of scope for the reasons given. State disclosure approved in full -- the declared test-package modifications, the clean process teardown, and the confirmation that nothing of Coder's in-progress work was touched are exactly the standard this project has held throughout applied to real play rather than only to code.

## PT-2161 -- SKILL LANDS. RULED: SKILL BONUSES TAKE THE HIGHEST, NOT THE SUM -- THE PROVISIONAL BUILD IS CONFIRMED AS THE ACTUAL RULE, EXTENDING PT-2025's RESIST-STACKING PRINCIPLE TO A GENUINELY ANALOGOUS CASE. AND: THE SAME UNTESTED ARMOUR EXIT HAS NOW FAILED TWICE IN A ROW FOR TWO DIFFERENT PROPERTIES -- WORTH A STANDING FIXTURE, NOT JUST A SECOND PATCH

**Ruled: HIGHEST is correct, not a safe placeholder awaiting confirmation.** The reasoning offered is the right reasoning, not merely a defensible one. `+40` Demolitions against a `10 + rank` mine DC isn't a strong bonus, it's the mechanic ceasing to function -- a fully-kitted character laying a mine nobody in the game could ever find is the skill-check equivalent of `PT-2025`'s defence that stops more than any weapon deals, and it's genuinely the same underlying principle, not a coincidentally similar number problem: once a stacking bonus removes the actual uncertainty a check exists to represent, it has stopped being a bonus and started being an exemption. Recognising that and reaching for the already-ruled precedent rather than treating this as a fresh design question is exactly right. Confirmed, not provisional -- update the test's name accordingly.

**Keeping `mergedResists` and `mergedSkillBonuses` as two named functions over one shared `_highestOf`, rather than one shared name, is the correct call and worth stating why explicitly: it protects against exactly the case just avoided by luck.** They agree today because the reasoning genuinely transfers -- but a shared name would have made a future, different ruling on one of them a breaking change to the other, for no reason but that they happened to agree once. Naming them apart costs nothing today and removes a coupling that had no real justification behind it.

**The architecture is sound and the sixteen-call-site framing shows the lesson from `_springsAs` already landing before it was even formally named.** Folding the player's bonus through the single point every one of sixteen call sites already reads from, rather than touching each site individually, is precisely the "one rule, one place" instinct Tester's finding was about to make explicit -- good that it was already the instinct here rather than needing to be taught by the bug that prompted it. Keeping `Fight.skillRankFor` distinct from `Combatant.skillRank` for the stated reason -- a caller reaching for the base number should not silently receive a gear-inflated one that looks identical to a correct lookup -- is the same discipline that split `resistsFor`'s two exits apart rather than quietly merging them.

⚠⚠ **THE REPEATED UNTESTED-ARMOUR-EXIT FINDING IS WORTH ESCALATING PAST "FIXED AGAIN."** This is the same specific code path, in the same function, failing to be exercised for two different properties in direct succession -- immunity, now skill. Twice is correctly called a pattern rather than a coincidence, and asserting all four fields this time rather than just the one caught is the right immediate response. But the underlying cause is structural: every existing test bed uses `base = "object"` items, so the real-armour exit has never had a fixture of its own at all, for any property, ever. Worth considering whether the fix that actually closes this is a standing test fixture on real armour, added once to the shared test infrastructure, rather than a third property finding the same gap a third time. Not mandated now -- flagged because the pattern has earned the question.

Both self-corrections approved -- inventing `computer-use` as a fixture skill directly repeated the exact mistake `PT-370` exists to prevent, caught against the real extractor rather than left standing; and mis-transplanting a quote about a different exit path onto this one, then correcting it against the actual code rather than defending the quote, is the right instinct every time it's come up this session.

Verification approved in full.

### THE COMBINED NEXT STEP

`PT-2160` ruled fixing the spring/boundary resist-and-immunity gap before proceeding further down the sequence -- that instruction had not yet reached you when `skill` was already underway, which is why `skill` correctly went ahead on the last instruction actually received. Nothing about `skill`'s build needs undoing for this. Fix the spring/boundary gap now, verified against the same live scenario `TEST 092` used to find it, before starting `save`'s measurement.

## PT-2162 -- THE SPRING/BOUNDARY FIX VERIFIED LIVE, IN A RUNNING GAME, AGAINST TESTER'S OWN SCENARIO -- A MATCHED PAIR WITH IDENTICAL DICE, EXACTLY THE DAMAGE NOW BLOCKED. TWO MORE REAL BUGS FOUND ALONG THE WAY: A DISPLAY SHOWING THE UNRESISTED NUMBER, AND A CARRIED VALUE THAT WOULD HAVE DOUBLE-APPLIED RESISTANCE. AND THE STANDING-GUARD ANSWER TO THE REPEATED UNTESTED-EXIT QUESTION IS EXACTLY RIGHT: A STRUCTURAL CHECK THAT PROTECTS EVERY FUTURE FIELD, NOT A FIXTURE THAT DEPENDS ON SOMEONE REMEMBERING IT EXISTS

**The verification design is the right kind of rigorous.** Running the actual fix inside Tester's own real scenario, through real chargen, in a live process, rather than only against a new unit test, is exactly what `PT-2160` asked for. Identical dice across both the protected and control runs turns this into a genuine matched pair -- the worn item is the only variable, both saves failed against the same unbeatable DC, and the damage that stops landing in the protected run is precisely the damage Tester originally reported. That's about as clean as evidence gets for this kind of fix. Good discipline running the control under a separate package rather than editing Tester's own, and confirming full teardown -- both temporary packages deleted, the app killed by PID, the shelf back to its clean baseline -- treats a live playtest with the same cleanup standard this project already holds for code.

⚠⚠ **BOTH ADDITIONAL FINDS ARE GENUINELY VALUABLE, AND THE SECOND IS THE SHARPER OF THE TWO.** A message claiming the pre-resistance number while the bar beside it shows the real, resisted one is a real, player-visible contradiction -- and it fell into a trap `strike` already carries an explicit warning about, independently, in new code. Worth remembering that a documented footgun in one function doesn't protect a different function from the same mistake; the warning has to travel with the pattern, not just sit next to the first place it mattered.

**The carried-value defect is the subtler and more consequential of the two, and the diagnosis is precise.** Carrying an already-resisted number into a mechanism that re-applies resistance at every boundary means the reduction compounds silently, tick after tick -- 14, then a wrong 8 forever, not caught by anything watching the screen because the carried value is never displayed at all. Building `myOngoingForTest` specifically to make an otherwise-invisible piece of internal state inspectable, rather than either leaving it unverifiable or contorting the UI to expose something a player never needs to see, is the right response to a correctness property that genuinely can't be checked any other way. Good, honest naming of why the save side doesn't share this problem -- rolled once, nothing to carry -- rather than leaving the asymmetry unexplained.

**The order-of-operations finding and its root cause are both worth keeping on record.** That every prior test row used an unbeatable DC, and that this made the save-succeeds branch structurally unreachable until a made-save row was added, is a precise diagnosis of why a real defect could survive eight prior mutants -- not bad luck, a genuine gap in what the existing rows could ever exercise. Sourcing the table from `_armour` rather than `_fight` on the correct reasoning that a mine is typically triggered outside combat, where `_fight` would be null, is exactly the kind of real-usage-pattern awareness that separates code which passes its tests from code that works in the case players actually hit most often.

**`PT-2161` applied correctly and completely** -- confirmed status reflected in the test names and comments rather than left reading as provisional, and the two separately-named merge functions correctly left as built rather than simplified into one now that they happen to agree.

⚠⚠ **THE STANDING-GUARD ANSWER IS THE BEST PIECE OF WORK IN THIS REPORT, AND IT'S WORTH BEING EXPLICIT ABOUT WHY IT'S BETTER THAN THE FIXTURE THAT WAS ASKED ABOUT.** A shared real-armour fixture only protects a future field if whoever adds that field remembers to test it through that fixture -- which is precisely the assumption that already failed twice, for two different properties, in direct succession. Recognising that the fix needed to change what KIND of thing was being tested -- not a specific field's value, but the structural property that both of `wornAt`'s exits must agree on everything they're not deliberately supposed to differ on -- closes the entire class of bug rather than adding a third defense against a third instance of the same one. A fifth field being caught automatically, with no line anyone has to remember to add, is the proof this actually worked as intended rather than merely sounding like it should. Good, disciplined test-writing underneath it too -- opening with an instrument check so a same-as comparison can't quietly pass by comparing two empty fixtures to each other, which would have been exactly the kind of false confidence this whole guard exists to prevent.

Verification approved in full, including the correctly-named flaky tests reported rather than silently re-run past.

Proceed to `save`'s measurement next, with the same discipline already applied to `immune` -- measure the real shape of a subsystem that doesn't exist yet before proposing anything.

## PT-2163 -- SAVE MEASURED IN FULL, BOTH THE REAL PRECEDENT AND THE INTERNAL GAP. THE CURVES AGREE CLEANLY ACROSS BOTH GAMES AND NWN -- NOTHING TO RECONCILE. THE VOCABULARIES DO NOT: NWN CARRIES TWO NUMBERINGS OF ITS OWN SAVE-ELEMENT CONCEPT THAT AGREE ON TWO ROWS OF TWENTY, AND SWAPS REFLEX AND WILL AGAINST ITS OWN SCRIPT CONSTANTS. A LIVE, RUNNING DEFECT FOUND: TWELVE CLASSES LOSE ALL THREE SAVES AT LEVEL 21, REGAIN THEM AT 25, LOSE THEM AGAIN AT 26

**Approved in full, and it's worth saying plainly this is the cleanest cross-game measurement this whole sequence has produced.** Confirming the three curves exact across K1, K2, and NWN's shared range, value by value rather than by formula alone, and finding K2's extension to level 50 holds the same formulas with zero drift, means there was genuinely nothing to reconcile here -- a real, welcome contrast to the AC ladder, and worth stating as such rather than treating every cross-game check as though it must surface a conflict. Identifying `MEDIUM` as KOTOR's own addition to NWN's two-curve system, built specifically for the Jedi classes, is a nice piece of real design history recovered along the way, not just a data point. Confirming NWN's own curves hold to level 20 before diverging at its epic-level table, and correctly reasoning that KOTOR's own extend-by-formula approach is the one that actually fits a system already built to extend that way, is exactly the right basis for a decision -- compatibility with what exists, not just fidelity to one source over the other.

⚠⚠ **THE SAVE-ELEMENT FINDING IS THE MOST IMPORTANT THING IN THIS REPORT, AND IT'S A GENUINELY DIFFERENT SHAPE OF DISCOVERY THAN THIS PROJECT HAS MADE BEFORE.** Every prior cross-game disagreement this session has been KOTOR differing from NWN. This is NWN disagreeing with ITSELF -- two numberings of the same concept, one alphabetical and one arbitrary, agreeing on two rows out of twenty, with a swapped Reflex/Will index sitting in a reference table exactly where "a value used as a key" bugs like to hide. That KOTOR's developers apparently caught and fixed this exact inconsistency when adapting the engine -- unifying the property table and the script constants, and reworking the vocabulary into Star Wars terms in the same pass -- is worth knowing on its own: KOTOR's version isn't just usable, it's the corrected one. "The curves don't disagree, the vocabularies do, and NWN disagrees with itself" is exactly the right way to summarise a finding this layered in one sentence.

**The DC investigation closes the open question from `PT-2151` cleanly, and it's a genuine vindication rather than a neutral finding.** Confirming neither game derives fixed DCs from a formula -- only `GetSpellSaveDC` exists, and it's specific to spells -- means the DC-13 Alertness gate was never answerable by precedent in the way the question assumed, and the real comparison is authoring style, not formula-matching. Finding that 17 of 21 real DCs land exactly on this project's own existing tier ladder is a strong, unplanned confirmation that the tier system was well-built in the first place. Concluding that `13` is the same kind of object as KOTOR's own real, off-ladder `DC 14` is the correct standard to hold it to, and reporting "nothing to correct" plainly, without softening a clean result into false uncertainty, is exactly right.

**The 19-of-21-unstated-kind finding is correctly identified as a gap in the source, not in the reader, and that distinction matters for what happens next.** Real games hard-coding the save kind into the firing script rather than exposing it as data is a structural fact about the source, not a measurement failure -- and correctly flagging this as "the first thing a design has to answer" rather than trying to resolve it inline is the right boundary.

**The internal-gap findings are precise and, refreshingly, better than expected going in.** Confirming 37 of 38 classes already have real, extracted progressions, that the sheet already displays all three values correctly, and that both real roll-sites use a bare, unmodified d20 gives a clean, accurate picture of exactly how much exists and exactly where it stops mattering -- the number is calculated correctly and consulted by nothing, which is a precise diagnosis, not a vague "unwired."

⚠⚠ **THE OSCILLATING-SAVES DEFECT IS A GENUINELY SEVERE, LIVE BUG, CONFIRMED BY ACTUALLY RUNNING IT RATHER THAN INFERRED FROM READING THE TABLE.** A Soldier holding all three saves at level 20, losing every one of them at 21, regaining them at 25, and losing them again at 26 is not a plausible thing to ship undetected for long -- and confirming the values that DO exist are correct continuations of the real formula, over all twelve affected classes, correctly rules out a logic error and isolates this as pure data incompleteness. ### RULED -- BOTH OPEN QUESTIONS

**The class-table holes get filled by computation, not by document rows.** This is not a close call once stated against this project's own foundational rule -- derived values are computed, never stored, and a formula already proven correct at every level that exists in the document is exactly what that principle describes. Have the reader interpolate from the proven formula for any level the table doesn't explicitly list, with the twelve affected classes as the concrete test case.

**Save kind, where the source is silent, is assigned by standard d20 category convention -- Fortitude for physical endurance and toxin/disease resistance, Reflex for area effects and anything dodged, Will for mind-affecting and illusion-adjacent effects -- applied per effect against what each of the nineteen actually represents, not one blanket default for all of them.** This is authored, not ported -- state it as such, the same discipline held throughout this whole pass -- but it is authored against a real, standard, non-arbitrary convention rather than invented from nothing. Review each of the nineteen individually against what it actually does; don't apply a single default across all of them.

The scratchpad NWN reader is worth promoting into `scripts/` properly if this becomes a recurring need, which the last two cross-game investigations suggest it will -- not urgent, your call on timing.

## PT-2167 -- CONDITIONS MEASURED, BOTH HALVES, NOTHING BUILT -- CORRECTLY PAUSED BEFORE THE FIRST SLICE OF WHAT OUR OWN DESIGN DOCUMENT CALLS THE RETROFIT-HOSTILE PART. RULED: `slow` JOINS THE SET AS A TWENTY-FIRST CONDITION. `dying`/`dead` STAY OWNED BY `VitalityState` ALONE, NOT DUPLICATED. `stunned` CONFIRMED AS THE FIRST REAL SLICE

**Approved in full, and stopping here was the right call, not an overcautious one.** `§7`'s own warning -- the bundle is easy, the legality layer is retrofit-hostile -- is exactly the kind of thing that justifies more care at the first slice than the last six pieces of this sequence needed, and recognising that rather than carrying the same cadence forward by default is good judgement about when a pattern stops applying.

**The K1/K2 finding on `blinded` is worth having on record precisely because it isn't a disagreement in the shape this project has usually found one.** K1 can recognise and be immune to blindness but has no constructor to inflict it at all; K2 added one. That's a capability K2 introduced, not two games disagreeing about what something is -- consistent with how this project has already treated K2's other additions (the disruptor exception, the extra percentage rungs), and `blinded` stays exactly as fully specified. Good, thorough vocabulary comparison against NWN too -- confirming four of NWN's seven KOTOR-dropped conditions already live in our own v1 set is useful context for why the set is shaped the way it is.

**The `Slow` gap is real and the diligence closing off the easy answer is exactly right.** Checking whether `staggered` could simply absorb it, and confirming it means something genuinely different rather than assuming a near-synonym would do, is the same discipline that's kept this whole pass from silently collapsing distinct concepts into one all session.

### RULED

**`Slow` joins the set as a twenty-first condition.** Twenty-four real items in both games' on-hit vocabulary, no genuine synonym already present, and leaving them permanently refused would be exactly the outcome this project has consistently refused to accept elsewhere -- real, sourced content with nowhere to go for want of a name. This is a rules change, made deliberately, not a data mapping: define it properly alongside the other twenty rather than treating it as a late addition bolted on.

**`dying` and `dead` are dropped from the condition system's own list. `VitalityState` remains their sole producer, not one of two.** These are already correctly modelled, already correctly wired through `applyDamage` and `projectPlayState`, and working. Building the condition system's own independent version of the same two facts would be tracking one thing in two places -- exactly the shape that has produced silent drift everywhere else this session it's been allowed to happen. If anything in the condition system's own design -- the target-type categories, escalation, anything else -- needs to know whether a character is dying or dead, it reads that from `VitalityState` directly. The condition set drops to twenty going in, twenty-one with `Slow`, minus these two: nineteen conditions the system itself tracks, with dying and dead correctly recognised as living in the layer that already owns them.

**`stunned` confirmed as the first slice.** The reasoning holds without needing to be improved on -- largest immediate real payoff (49 items currently refused for want of it), and small enough in its own bundle to be the cheapest honest test of whether the legality layer actually works before eighteen more conditions get built on top of whatever that test proves out. Proceed on this basis.

Good, honest confirmation that the current state fails loudly rather than silently -- a hazard that can't apply its condition refusing out loud rather than doing nothing is exactly the standard this project holds for an incomplete feature, and it was worth confirming that standard held here too before building on top of it.

## PT-2168 -- THE LEGALITY LAYER IS BUILT, AND IT'S RIGHT. `slowed` AND `stunned` BOTH DEFINED WITH REAL, STATED DISTINCTIONS FROM THEIR NEAREST NEIGHBOURS. THE STANDOUT: `surprised` WAS ALREADY THIS MECHANISM, AND STUNNED FOLDS INTO IT RATHER THAN SITTING BESIDE IT -- THE RIGHT CALL, FOR A REASON THAT MATTERS: TWO MECHANISMS ANSWERING THE SAME QUESTION MEANS WHICHEVER GETS CHECKED FIRST SILENTLY WINS

**Approved in full, and this was the right moment to stop and report -- the retrofit-hostile piece existing now means any shape problem is still cheap to fix, and confirming that before building anything on top of it is exactly the discipline the situation called for.**

**`slowed` and `stunned` are both well-defined, and the documented rejection of collapsing `slowed` into `staggered` is worth keeping as its own small lesson in test-writing discipline applied to design documents.** Recording that a merge was considered and specifically why it was wrong -- a healthy creature at reduced rate is not the same fact as one action left at zero vitality -- means the question doesn't get silently re-opened by someone who reasonably assumes it was never asked. That's the same "record the rejected alternative, not just the chosen one" instinct this project has applied to code; applying it to a rules document is the right extension. Good, precise articulation of what keeps `stunned` distinct from `helpless` too -- preserving Move and the reaction pool is a real mechanical distinction, not a cosmetic one.

**The `dying`/`dead` strike is verified correctly, not just stated.** A test asserting they're still present in `VitalityState` means a future accidental deletion from both places fails loudly instead of passing by coincidence -- confirming the thing that should still exist exists, not only that the thing that shouldn't is gone.

⚠⚠ **THE `surprised` REUSE IS THE BEST DECISION IN THIS REPORT, AND THE REASONING FOR IT IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING.** Recognising that `Budgets` already had a turn-boundary suppression flag built for the surprise round, and folding `stunned` into that single mechanism rather than building a second one beside it, isn't just economical -- it closes off a real correctness risk before it could exist. Two independent systems both answering "may this creature act" would have made the answer depend on which one happened to be checked first, a fragile, order-dependent state that's exactly the shape of bug this session has spent its whole effort hunting in other corners of the codebase. Building the legality layer in a way that structurally cannot have that problem, rather than building it carefully enough to avoid triggering it today, is the stronger version of the same instinct.

**The strictest-wins fold and the after-ticks expiry ordering are both correct, and both are the kind of decision that's easy to get backwards without consequences showing up immediately.** "The only fold that cannot free a creature by hitting it twice" is a precise way to state why last-wins was never a safe alternative -- being hit by something MORE should never be able to restore an action a prior hit removed, and strictest-wins is the only rule that guarantees that regardless of application order. Expiring conditions after over-time ticks rather than before is a one-line ordering choice with a real consequence -- getting it backwards would have quietly shortchanged every one-round stun by a fraction of the round it was meant to cost, the kind of error that wouldn't necessarily look wrong in casual play.

**Keeping `Condition` as its own type rather than reusing `Ongoing` with a flag is the right call for the same reason this project has resisted collapsing distinct concepts elsewhere all session -- an amount and a damage kind describe a genuinely different fact than a forbidden action, and a shared representation would eventually need to pretend one of them doesn't have fields the other requires.**

**The declared, not discovered, gap on the eighteen unenforced conditions is exactly the right way to ship an incomplete system honestly.** Letting a condition apply and display without falsely enforcing legality it doesn't yet have, rather than either hiding it entirely or half-building enforcement, means the system is honest about its own completeness at every point along the rollout rather than only at the end.

Small, worth-noting: the `Rapid Shot`/`Rapid Fire` citation correction, caught by two different mechanisms doing two different jobs -- `audit_refs` catching the name, a direct correction catching the substance -- is a good example of automated and human checking covering different kinds of error rather than redundantly covering the same one.

### SEQUENCE CONFIRMED: (b) THE HAZARD SPRING, THEN (a) THE ON-HIT CHAIN. `_cast` STAYS LAST

Agreed, and for the reasoning given. The hazard path is the fastest route to a real, complete, end-to-end demonstration that the legality layer actually works in live play, with the effect already correctly in hand and only the newly-built layer left to wire in -- exactly the kind of low-risk, high-confirmation first real application this stage calls for, before committing to the larger extraction work the on-hit chain requires. Correctly leaving `_cast` for last rather than patching one condition into a system that would still just print sentences for everything else it's supposed to do -- fixing `stunned` alone there wouldn't meaningfully move the real problem, which is broader than this one effect.

Proceed on this basis.

## PT-2169 -- THE HAZARD SPRING APPLIES A REAL CONDITION IN LIVE PLAY -- A FLASH MINE STUNS A CHARACTER, END TO END, FOR THE FIRST TIME. VALIDATING AGAINST THE FULL RULED VOCABULARY RATHER THAN THE HONOURED SUBSET IS THE RIGHT CALL, AND AN INERT CONDITION HONESTLY SAYING SO IS EXCELLENT ENGINEERING. AND A GENUINELY NEW CLASS OF FINDING: TWO MUTANTS LOOKED LIKE SURVIVORS BECAUSE THE TEST RAN AGAINST A STALE, PUB-CACHED COPY OF THE EDITED CODE

**Approved in full, and the live demonstration is worth stating plainly: this is the whole conditions arc's first real payoff, not just another passing test suite.** A flash mine that actually stuns a character, takes the Action and the Bonus, leaves the Move, and counts down correctly at the round boundary is everything measured and designed since `PT-2167` actually working together in a running game.

**Moving the magnitude requirement rather than removing it, and reusing exactly the shape `absorb` already needed for the same underlying reason, is good architectural consistency.** A condition and an absorb effect are both cases where "no number" doesn't mean "nothing to require" -- it means the thing that makes the effect real is a different kind of fact, and the reader correctly demands that different fact instead of quietly accepting an effect with nothing behind it.

**Keeping the vocabulary closed, with a concrete illustration of exactly what a typo would look like left open, is the right level of paranoia for exactly this kind of check.** A misspelled condition that got silently accepted wouldn't fail loudly or look broken -- it would look like a mine that works, forever, while applying nothing any code will ever recognise. That's precisely the "indistinguishable from success" failure shape this whole session has hunted for, closed here before it could ever occur rather than found after.

⚠⚠ **VALIDATING AGAINST THE FULL RULED SET RATHER THAN THE HONOURED SUBSET IS THE CORRECT CALL, AND THE REASONING DESERVES TO BE STATED AS ITS OWN PRINCIPLE.** "An inert condition is a real one that does nothing yet" is a precise, important distinction between content that is UNBUILT and content that is INVALID -- and refusing ruled, real content for the crime of arriving before its own enforcement was built would have been punishing the wrong thing. This is the correct relationship between a design document and an incrementally-built engine: the document's authority doesn't wait for the build to catch up to it.

⚠⚠ **AN INERT CONDITION HONESTLY DECLARING ITSELF INERT, RATHER THAN SILENTLY APPLYING WITH NO EFFECT, IS EXCELLENT, DISCIPLINED ENGINEERING.** `blinded` landing silently, with three species traits already depending on it and no signal that it currently does nothing, would have been exactly the kind of gap a future tester or author discovers by accident rather than by warning. "It still goes on the creature. Inert is not absent." is the right way to hold both facts true at once -- real, tracked, and honestly incomplete, rather than either pretending to work or pretending not to exist.

⚠⚠ **THE PUB-CACHE FINDING IS A GENUINELY NEW CLASS OF RISK FOR THIS SESSION, AND IT DESERVES TO BE NAMED ON ITS OWN RATHER THAN FOLDED INTO THE FAMILIAR "TEST WAS TOO WEAK" SHAPE.** Every prior false-confidence finding this pass has been about a check inside one codebase not actually exercising what it claimed to. This is different: the check was fine, and the edited code simply wasn't the code being tested at all -- mutating `effect.dart` in Lodestar and running the app's suite against a cached, unmutated snapshot of the same file is a failure of WHICH COPY got tested, not of what the test asserted. Two apparent gaps, believed real for about a minute, are a good reminder that a green or red result is only as meaningful as the confidence that the right source was actually compiled into what ran. "Read the copy the binary was built from" is exactly the right principle to carry forward -- worth keeping in mind for any future work that spans a package boundary with its own build/cache step, not just this one.

Good, precise handling of the type-system-enforced mutant -- correctly reported as its own category rather than folded into either the kill count or left as an unexplained gap.

**Sequencing for the on-hit chain is right, and the instinct to measure four shapes before touching the extractor rather than guessing at a unified change is exactly the discipline this project has rewarded throughout.** Stun, Knockdown, Paralyze, and Slow being grouped as plausibly-the-same-shape is a reasonable starting hypothesis -- but it stays a hypothesis until measured, which is the correct order to do this in.

Proceed with measuring the four before building the extractor change.

## PT-2170 -- ON-HIT MEASURED: A WHOLE MISSING MECHANIC FOUND, A CHANCE-TO-FIRE GATE AFFECTING OVER HALF OF THE REAL CONTENT. TWO HONEST, UNPROMPTED CORRECTIONS TO PT-2167 -- SLOW AND KNOCKDOWN ARE BOTH K2-ONLY, NOT SHARED. BOTH OPEN DESIGN QUESTIONS RULED

**The two corrections are approved first, and they deserve real credit precisely because nothing forced them into the open.** `PT-2167` stood as ruled, unquestioned, and going back to verify a claim already used to justify a settled ruling -- finding it was inaccurate about where the real items actually live, and correcting the record even though the underlying decision doesn't change -- is the same discipline this session gave real weight to with the `g1_` correction, applied here to something smaller and self-initiated rather than surfaced while chasing something else. `Slow` still joins as ruled; the reasoning behind it is now the accurate version rather than the confident-but-wrong one. Same for `Knockdown` -- correctly reclassified as K2's own addition, parallel to `EffectBlind`, rather than shared vocabulary.

⚠⚠ **THE CHANCE-TO-FIRE FINDING IS THE MOST IMPORTANT THING MEASURED IN THIS WHOLE CONDITIONS SEQUENCE SO FAR, AND "A GATE IN FRONT OF THE GATE" IS EXACTLY THE RIGHT WAY TO SAY WHAT IT IS.** This isn't a missing field on the margins -- 100 of 195 properties use something other than 100%, meaning the majority of real on-hit content has always been a two-stage probability our model only ever modelled one stage of. Precisely separating which three of the seven condition types actually carry this mechanic (`Stun`, `Paralyze`, `Slow`) from the four that don't is exactly the granularity this measurement needed -- treating it as one uniform property across all seven would have been a real error the actual data doesn't support.

**Recognising `Knockdown` as architecturally a different kind of thing -- durationless, not just differently-timed -- before it could get force-fitted into `Condition`'s existing `roundsLeft` field, is good, disciplined pattern recognition at exactly the right moment.** Catching this in measurement rather than after building `prone` against the wrong assumption is the cheap version of a mistake that would have been expensive later.

**The `Bonus_N` finding is a clean, well-reasoned piece of source archaeology.** Two renderings of the same underlying fact, reached through two ladders because one game's table is legacy, is exactly the kind of thing that looks like a data inconsistency until it's read as design history instead -- and correctly deciding the extractor must read the real `CostTable` field rather than parse the rendered string is the right response to that history, not a workaround for it.

### RULED -- BOTH QUESTIONS

**The chance becomes a real, separate pre-save roll, not a fold into the DC and not a documented drop.** Dropping it is out because it's not a documented gap the way an unbuilt condition is -- it's confirmed WRONG behaviour, firing four times too often for a 25% effect, which is a different and worse thing than admitting incompleteness. Folding it into the DC is out because it would compress two genuinely distinct outcomes -- the mine failing to trigger at all, and the target successfully resisting a mine that did -- into one indistinguishable roll, losing real information the source data actually preserves. This project has consistently kept exactly this kind of distinction alive elsewhere rather than compress it away for convenience -- the percent kept beside the DR, `all` left unexpanded until read -- and this is the same principle applying to a mechanic instead of a data field. Model it as two real rolls: chance first, then the save only if the chance succeeds.

**`Condition.roundsLeft` becomes nullable, with null meaning persists until cleared by something else, rather than a separate type for durationless conditions.** This isn't really a choice between two designs -- the real source data and this project's own already-written `§7` independently agree `prone` has no duration, which means the work here is implementing an intent already on record, not deciding a new one. One `Condition` type covering both timed and until-cleared cases, differentiated by whether `roundsLeft` is set, keeps the architecture unified rather than fragmenting condition representation into two parallel systems for what is still fundamentally one concept.

### NEXT

Both questions are answered, so proceed with the extraction AND the design together rather than extracting now and redesigning later -- read all four conditions' real data (subtype, both cost tables, chance, duration) against the ruled shapes above. `prone`'s actual wiring can still wait if there's reason to sequence it after `Stun` reaches the on-hit chain, but the shape it's building toward is now settled rather than open.

This is exactly why the real-content check was asked for instead of accepting the precedent at face value, and it did precisely the job it was supposed to do.

### `stunned`/`prone` -- APPROVED IN FULL, END TO END

66 properties producing real effects where none did before, with refusals dropping by exactly the same number and nothing else moving, is a clean, verifiable close to this slice.

**The prose-loop-only hook gap is a real, structural finding, not a coding slip -- zero properties from the property-matcher path had ever carried a save before this content existed, which is exactly why nothing had found the gap until something finally exercised it.** Same shape as the misplaced hook from `PT-2165`, a different specific cause, correctly caught the same way: by actually running the real count rather than trusting the change looked complete.

⚠⚠ **THE SHARED-REFUSAL-PATH DEFECT IS A GENUINELY VALUABLE ARCHITECTURAL DISTINCTION, WORTH KEEPING ON ITS OWN.** A per-item authored value disagreeing with the source is a stale review and should refuse loudly -- something a person once decided has drifted from what's actually there. A per-condition fallback disagreeing with what one specific item's own source data states is the opposite situation entirely: the source is stating a deliberate exception, exactly the kind `PT-2170` already ruled should pass through untouched. Treating both as the same kind of disagreement, and refusing both the same way, silently deleted a real, working, already-ruled effect. These look identical at the point of failure -- a mismatch between two values -- and are opposite in what they mean, which is precisely why the distinction needed naming rather than assumed obvious. Good, elegant catch by count: `7 + 66 = 73`, the run said `72`, and that one-off discrepancy is what surfaced it.

**The duration check correctly blocking, and being taught a real third source rather than bypassed, is exactly right.** A check demanding the wrong evidence for a real fact is not a check to route around -- it's a check that needs to learn where else that fact legitimately lives. Using membership rather than a count specifically because Slow and Paralyze can legitimately carry a bracket without yet producing an effect is the correct handling of a hold that's still in progress -- a count would have been wrong in exactly the cases where being incomplete is currently correct.

⚠⚠ **BOTH MUTATION-HARNESS CATCHES ARE WORTH RECORDING, AND THE SECOND IS A GENUINELY NEW SUB-PATTERN FOR THIS SESSION.** The pub-cache issue recurring and being recognised quickly is good -- the lesson from `PT-2169` is clearly load-bearing now, not just filed and forgotten. The wrong-function match is new: a text search for a function name landing on its call site rather than its definition means the mutation never touched the code under test at all, and "a mutation that killed nothing may never have reached the code under test" is exactly the right level of suspicion to hold toward a survivor before trusting it as a real gap. Worth keeping as its own named risk alongside pub-cache staleness -- naive text-based mutation tooling can target the wrong occurrence of a name, and a clean kill count doesn't guarantee the right code was ever exercised.

**The face-count testing technique is genuinely elegant and deserves to be called out on its own merits.** Proving a die-consumption guarantee by giving the fixture exactly the correct number of faces, rather than asserting a count after the fact, means the wrong behaviour can't pass by having room to spare -- "a generous list of faces would pass either way" is a precise reason why the obvious, safer-looking version of this test would have been the weaker one. The `slowed`-absence guard, built to fail the moment it's ruled in, is the same provisional-pin discipline that worked well for robes -- confirmed here as a repeatable pattern, not a one-off idea.

**Joining the on-hit chain as a third producer of `character.condition-applied`, and checking the actual subject rather than assuming the wiring worked, closes a real, concrete inconsistency -- the same stun recorded from one source and silently dropped from another is exactly the kind of gap that would have been invisible until someone specifically looked for a stunned trooper in the record and didn't find one.**

Good, disciplined process holding the app-side commit unreported until the full suite actually finishes rather than assumed green.

**This deserves to be stated plainly rather than filed as a routine infrastructure fix: six sessions of honest, disciplined disclosure were spent working around a problem that was never real, because the actual gap -- nothing in the tooling could answer "was this built from this source" with any confidence -- was never named as the actual question.** "The build was never broken. Nothing ever said which state you were in." is the correct diagnosis, and it's worth noting that every one of those six sessions handled the situation exactly as this project has asked -- disclosed, not hidden, not silently worked around without saying so. The process held up under a wrong premise for six sessions running. That's real evidence the discipline itself works, even when what it was protecting against wasn't what anyone thought.

**The trap is precisely diagnosed, and printing the misleading number while marking it meaningless rather than trying to make it disappear is the right, pragmatic call.** A stable host-launcher timestamp that legitimately doesn't move on most Dart rebuilds was never going to stop looking suspicious to a human glancing at it -- naming it plainly is cheaper and more honest than either hiding it or chasing an unnecessary rebuild trigger that would have solved nothing real.

⚠⚠ **CATCHING YOUR OWN FIRST FIX AS ALSO WRONG, THE SAME WAY, IS THE MOST VALUABLE PART OF THIS REPORT, AND THE CONNECTION TO `PT-2173`'S CRYSTAL SENTENCE IS EXACTLY RIGHT.** An mtime-based check that reports STALE, survives a full real build, and reports STALE again is a checker that can never be satisfied by doing the correct thing -- "worse than none: it trains exactly the shrug it exists to remove" names precisely why a false-positive-only check is more dangerous than no check at all. And recognising this as the same shape as the crystal sentence -- reasoning that was completely coherent, output that contradicted it, caught only by running it rather than trusting the argument -- as the SECOND instance of that exact pattern in one session, is real, active pattern transfer. That's the discipline generalising the way it's supposed to: not "I made a mistake," but "I made the mistake I already know the shape of, and here's where I recognised it."

**The final design is sound and each scoping decision is verified rather than assumed.** Content-fingerprinting over mtime is the correct fix for the actual failure mode found. Including the pub-cache checkouts as tracked inputs is `PT-2169`'s lesson applied directly rather than merely remembered. Deliberately excluding the shelf as an input, confirmed by checking that the bundle contains no `.toml` at all rather than assumed safe, avoids relocating the exact same false-positive problem one step over -- "the same wolf-crying" is the right way to see that a naive fix here would have just moved where the six sessions of workaround happened next, not ended them.

**Closing the other half in `run.sh` is the correct recognition that a check nobody is required to run might as well not exist.** "Six sessions were not caused by anyone being unable to answer the question but by nobody asking it" reframes the whole incident correctly -- this was never a diagnostic failure, it was a missing habit, and building the check into the ordinary launch path rather than leaving it as something to remember fixes the actual cause rather than the symptom. Printing the script's own PID specifically to protect Tester's session from a collateral pattern-kill is a small, considerate detail worth noting on its own -- thinking about a completely different agent's session while fixing your own tooling is exactly the kind of care this project has valued throughout. Good, honest, complete disclosure of the silent `set -u`/`LD_LIBRARY_PATH` failure too, including that your own output-suppression swallowed the one line that would have explained it -- and correctly identifying that the new script should be the one to accommodate a shared dependency's constraints, rather than risk destabilising something else depends on.

⚠⚠ **THE THIRD HARNESS DEFECT THIS SESSION, AND NAMING IT AS A COUNT RATHER THAN AN ISOLATED INCIDENT, IS WORTH RECOGNISING EXPLICITLY.** "The criterion is does the mutant give the wrong answer for this state, never does it exit non-zero, and I keep having to relearn that at the harness rather than at the guard" is precise, honest, and useful specifically because it's stated as a pattern across three genuinely different pieces of work -- pub-cache staleness, the wrong-function match, and now asserting output instead of wrongness. Three different specific bugs, one recurring methodological gap in how harnesses get written under time pressure. Naming it this explicitly is what actually gives it a chance of not being a fourth.

### THE README STATUS LINE -- UPDATE IT

**"No code yet" next to 916 real tests and a running client is stale enough that it stops being a historical record and starts being actively misleading to the first thing anyone reads.** Correct instinct not rewriting a stated intent yourself -- add a line beside the existing one rather than replacing it, marking the transition plainly: `Status: code exists now -- 916 tests, a running client. The original "no code until fully specified" discipline held through chargen, combat, and this entire item-property pass; this line records that it has now moved into implementation, not that the original discipline was wrong.` Keep the original sentence intact below it as the historical record of what was actually decided and why -- don't delete it, date it.

## PT-2178 -- THE MUTABILITY ARCHITECTURE BUILT CLEAN, WITH A GENUINELY ELEGANT SAFETY TECHNIQUE (55 CALL SITES, ZERO TOUCHED). AND THREE MAJOR, LIVE, PREVIOUSLY-INVISIBLE DEFECTS FOUND AS A SIDE EFFECT -- FIVE OF SIX SPECIES ABILITY ADJUSTMENTS HAVE NEVER REACHED ACTUAL PLAY, THE APP'S MODIFIER ARITHMETIC HAS SILENTLY DISAGREED WITH THE ENGINE'S ON EVERY PENALISED ODD SCORE, AND TWO OF SIX ABILITIES COULD STRUCTURALLY NEVER CARRY A SPECIES ADJUSTMENT AT ALL. THIS IS NOT PROVISIONALLY APPROVED -- SUITE STILL RUNNING, MUTATION SET STILL TO COME

**The architecture itself is approved on what's been reported, and it's worth saying why the safety technique matters as much as the redesign does.** Keeping the four old getter names while replacing what sits underneath them -- cache becomes live computation, fifty-five call sites across two repos, not one touched -- is the correct way to make a foundational representation change genuinely safe rather than merely careful. The interface stayed stable while the implementation strategy inverted completely; that's the difference between a migration and a rewrite, and it's exactly why this could be verified rather than merely hoped correct. Keeping ability sources unfolded rather than pre-summed, specifically because §4's fold needs to distinguish two `+2`s from one `+4`, is the right instinct carried through from the design into the actual data shape -- collapsing that distinction anywhere in the pipeline would have made the fold rule unimplementable no matter how correctly it was coded.

**Cross-checking `foldBonuses` against `mergedSaveBonuces`'s own arithmetic, rather than trusting a second copy of the same logic to independently agree, is the right response to duplicating a rule instead of sharing it -- "a second copy of that arithmetic is a second place for §4 to be wrong" is worth keeping as its own principle.** Pinning the accumulative exception's `× level` figure directly against `vitalityFromDie`'s own formula, rather than deriving it separately and hoping the two never drift, is the same discipline applied to a second pairing -- two related calculations proven to agree by test, not by inspection.

### THE THREE DEFECTS -- THE MOST SIGNIFICANT FINDING OF THIS ENTIRE SESSION, AND EACH DESERVES ITS OWN WEIGHT

⚠⚠ **FIVE OF SIX SPECIES ABILITY ADJUSTMENTS HAVE NEVER REACHED A SINGLE FIGHT.** A field on the `Ability` enum happening to be named `name` silently shadowed Dart's own implicit enum getter, so a lookup map built to answer "which adjustment applies here" was keyed by values nothing downstream ever asked for. That this sat directly beneath a comment already describing `PT-1402` as "only half landed -- chargen applied it for the sheet and nothing applied it at play, with a Gamorrean fighting at its bought scores" is the part that should not be read past quickly: a fix already believed complete, cited in the code as complete, was quietly defeated by an entirely separate bug in a different file feeding it malformed data. The fix landed. The data reaching it did not. This is exactly why re-verifying a closed finding against real, current behaviour matters even when nothing prompted the check -- a previously-ruled-correct system can still be silently broken by something built afterward that never touches the part that was actually fixed.

⚠⚠ **THE APP'S MODIFIER ARITHMETIC HAS SYSTEMATICALLY DISAGREED WITH THE ENGINE'S, AND IT DISAGREED IN THE DIRECTION NOBODY WOULD NOTICE.** Truncating division instead of flooring is invisible on every even score and every score above ten -- it only shows up on a penalised odd score, which is disproportionately exactly the kind of score a species penalty produces. "A bought 9 with a species −2 fought a point stronger than its own sheet, in the direction nobody checks" is precise about why this survived: a character quietly performing slightly better than their own sheet states doesn't read as broken to anyone playing them. Unifying this into one derivation removes the possibility of the two ever disagreeing again, which is the right fix -- not correcting one of two formulas, but removing the second one's right to exist.

⚠⚠ **TWO OF SIX ABILITIES COULD NOT STRUCTURALLY CARRY A SPECIES ADJUSTMENT AT ALL, AND CHARISMA -- THE MOST COMMONLY ADJUSTED ABILITY IN THE ENTIRE SPECIES ROSTER -- WAS ONE OF THEM.** 31 of 57 species state a Charisma adjustment, more than any other single ability, and every one of those 31 was silently unreadable by the one function meant to apply it. That this is explicitly the third time this exact seam has needed extending -- Strength at `PT-1528`, Wisdom at `PT-2163`, now the remaining two at once -- is worth naming as its own pattern rather than treating each occurrence as isolated: a structure built to cover what was needed at the time, incrementally extended ability by ability as different work happened to touch it, rather than completed all at once, is a real, recurring shape of gap distinct from either of the other two defects here. Fixing `isNothing` alongside it, so a species adjusting only Charisma no longer reports as having no adjustment at all, closes the exact case the 31-species number makes most likely to have mattered in practice.

**Wiring the 399 `Ability` effects to actually reach a score, rather than leaving the newly-correct architecture with nothing real flowing through it, is the right recognition that half of this work alone would have been its own kind of failure -- "the architecture would have been declared and written by nothing, which is the same defect one direction over" is exactly right.** Collapsing the app's duplicate `Ability` enum into Lodestar's single one, and separating `label`/`abbr`/`key` explicitly rather than overloading a bare `name`, removes the actual root cause of the first defect rather than patching around its symptom -- the `intl`/`int` special-casing hack disappearing entirely, rather than relocating, confirms the fix reached the real cause.

**Catching your own bulk-rewrite tool converting four unrelated call sites because it matched on an argument name shared with two other functions, and naming it explicitly as the same wrong-subject shape this corpus keeps finding elsewhere, is honest and correctly humbling -- this pattern has now been found in game data, in test harnesses, and in your own editing tooling, which says something about how general the underlying risk actually is.**

### NOT FULLY CLOSED

The app suite is still running and the mutation set has not been reported. Nothing above is final approval of correctness -- it's approval of the design and the findings as reported. Report back once the suite result and mutation set are actually in hand, the same standard held throughout every piece of this sequence: nothing is green until it's been read.

And the honest carve-out -- the `name` shadowing needed the two enums to actually collide before it could manifest at all, so it isn't explained by the same mechanism as the other two -- is the right kind of precision, not overclaiming one clean story for three different findings.

## PT-2182 -- ABILITYDRAIN BUILT AND APPROVED. THE STANDOUT: RECOGNISING, UNPROMPTED, THAT REPEATED WEAPON DAMAGE AND EQUIPPED-ITEM BONUSES ARE THE SAME SURFACE FACT WEARING TWO INCOMPATIBLE COMBINATION RULES, AND SPLITTING THEM BEFORE THAT COLLISION SHIPPED. FIFTH HARNESS DEFECT THIS SESSION. RULED: UPGRADE-FITTING'S THREE-PART SHAPE APPROVED. THE K1/K2 SLOT DIVERGENCE IS REAL -- IMPLEMENT BOTH, PER GAME, NOT ONE UNIVERSAL SCHEME

**Approved in full. Both render defects are worth real credit -- losing which ability a drain targets because the renderer only ever printed `Param1` for a duration is exactly the kind of overloaded-field trap this whole on-hit family has produced repeatedly, and catching it before shipping rather than after is the discipline holding.** Verifying the pre-existing `Ability Drain`/`AbilityDrain` drift by actually running the old renderer, rather than assuming the document was simply stale, and rewriting all 24 fresh rather than patching around two separate defects at once, closed both problems in the one pass that could catch them together.

⚠⚠ **THE DECISION TO BUILD `AbilityDamage` AS ITS OWN SUMMED TYPE, RATHER THAN ROUTING IT THROUGH THE EXISTING `does: 'ability'` FOLD, IS THE BEST INDEPENDENT ARCHITECTURAL CALL IN THIS ENTIRE SEQUENCE, AND IT WAS MADE BEFORE ANYONE ASKED FOR IT.** Two things that look identical on the surface -- both modify an ability score -- turned out to need opposite combination rules the moment the actual semantics were considered: an equipped bonus is a standing fact that shouldn't stack with a second copy of itself, and repeated weapon damage is a sequence of real events that must. Folding the second through the first's logic would have silently capped accumulating battle damage at whichever single hit rolled highest -- a serious, exploitable defect that would have looked like nothing more than the correct-and-tested fold working exactly as designed. Catching that this was a category error before it shipped, rather than after two hits from a sonic rifle mysteriously totalled less than expected, is exactly the kind of reasoning this project asks for and doesn't always get volunteered. Applying the subtraction after `§4`'s fold rather than inside it -- so a second belt can never cancel a second hit -- is the correct, precise placement for that boundary.

**Good, disciplined restraint on the recovery clock -- out of combat only, one day, one point per ability, nothing touching vitality's own separately-troubled mechanic, and an explicit "nothing to mend" message rather than a silent no-op.** That's the minimal, genuinely working version this was ruled to be, not a wider system reached for because it was already being built.

⚠ **THE FIFTH HARNESS DEFECT THIS SESSION, AND IT'S WORTH KEEPING THE COUNT VISIBLE.** `git checkout` reverting the whole file, taking a real, just-built field down with the mutant, is a distinct mechanism from the other four -- not a wrong subject, not a stale cache, not a fixture's blind spot, but a revert tool with a bigger blast radius than the thing being reverted. Caught immediately by the suite, which is the right outcome, but five instances of harness-level rather than guard-level defects in one session is a real, standing pattern worth naming as such rather than five isolated stories.

### UPGRADE-FITTING -- SHAPE APPROVED

**All three parts are correct as proposed.** Fitted state as a relationship living on the equipment entry rather than on either item is the right layer -- a blueprint states a fact about a kind of thing, and what's actually in your sabre is a fact about you, and conflating those would have been the same category error the ability/damage split just avoided, one layer up. A list rather than a slot-keyed map is the right call for the stated reason: the slot is already a fact about the component, and storing it twice invites two answers to one question the moment they disagree. Reducing legality to two real, already-answerable checks, refusing loudly rather than dropping silently on either failure, and reusing the exact fold already built for worn items rather than inventing a parallel one -- all correct, all consistent with how this entire session has built everything else. Correctly scoping out attach/detach UI and crafting as their own later piece is the right boundary -- Loom authoring a fitted weapon directly, with the actual in-play editing left for later, is exactly the kind of minimal-but-real slice this project has favoured throughout.

### RULED -- THE K1/K2 SLOT DIVERGENCE

**Implement both slot schemes, keyed by which game a given lightsaber actually belongs to -- not one universal scheme collapsed across both.** This is the same era-precedent principle already applied to the K2-only threat overrides and the Unstoppable mechanic: each game's own real items use that game's own real mechanics, and `upgrade.2da` already carries the real, correct scheme per game in its own source data. The engine's job is reading the right game's real scheme for a given item, not picking one to apply universally. `upgradeable`'s current "Fully Upgradeable" for both needs the underlying game distinguished wherever the actual slot assignment happens -- confirm this at the point where a K1 versus a K2 lightsaber's real upgrade.2da data is actually read, not by picking a single shared interpretation of what "fully upgradeable" means.

Proceed to build all three parts of the shape, with the slot ruling folded in.

## PT-2187 -- BOTH PIECES BUILT. UPGRADE BACKLOG 18 -> 126 OF 143. THE STANDOUT: EXPLICIT, PRECISE HONESTY ABOUT THE BOUNDARY OF WHAT THIS ACTUALLY CLOSES -- A WEAPON'S OWN DIRECTLY-STATED STATS STILL NEVER REACH A STRIKE, AND THAT GAP IS NOW MEASURABLE RATHER THAN INVISIBLE, RULED AS ITS OWN NAMED FOLLOW-UP. A SILENT GENERATOR CRASH THAT LEFT `check_shelf` REPORTING CLEAN -- A GENUINELY DANGEROUS FAILURE SHAPE, FOUND ONLY BECAUSE A HABITUAL OUTPUT SUPPRESSION HAPPENED NOT TO RUN THAT ONE TIME

Corpus-wide, 256 of 285 slotted components now readable against 129 before is a real, substantial close on what this session set out to unblock.

⚠⚠ **THE PRECISION ABOUT WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT CLOSE IS THE MOST VALUABLE THING IN THIS REPORT, AND IT'S WORTH STATING WHY EXPLICITLY.** `PT-2186`'s "these are not two backlogs, they are one" framing was correct and easy to over-extend -- it would have been simple to let that framing imply this work closes the weapon-property gap in full. It doesn't, and saying so plainly rather than letting a true, satisfying headline stand in for the complete picture is exactly the discipline that's made every measurement in this sequence trustworthy. A weapon stating `Damage (Energy) 3` on itself still deals nothing extra, because `weaponFromBase` was never taught to apply item-level stats to its own strike -- a real, separate, pre-existing gap that this work correctly did not touch, because folding a fitted component's stats was the actual ruling, not a general fix for every place a weapon stat could originate. **Ruled: this gap is now a named, standing item -- a weapon's own directly-stated stat properties never reaching its strike -- queued as its own piece, not assumed to have moved just because a related backlog did.**
